AN English Custom-house officer asked a traveller, "Anything to drink in that trunk of yours?" "No: only wearing apparel." Upon the trunk being searched, however, a dozen bottles of brandy were found. "Do you call these wearing apparel?" "Why, certainly—nightcape I " The trunk was passed. WHEN Sir George Rose was appointed one of the four judges of the now extinct Court of Review, he came to Lincoln's Inn with his colleagues to be sworn in. Some friend congratulating him on his access of dignity, he observed, "Yes, here we are, you see—four by honours?" A FRIEND meeting Sir George Rose one day in Lincolnis Inn Fields, with his left eye greatly swollen and inflamed, remonstrated with him, Adding that he was surprised Lady Rose should have letm go out of doors in such a condition. "Ah," replied Sir George, "I am out jure mariti" (my right eye). I.l!iii father of a young licentiate for the ministry went, no doubt with all the anxieties of a fond parent, to hear his son preach his first sermon. Another young man had been licensed at the same time, and the services of the day were shared between them. The father attended both, so that he might be able to form a comparison. On being asked his opinion of their respective merits, he replied—" He's really a nice young chiel' that was :preachin' i' the forenoon, an' has some spunk an ameddum in him ; but dear ane, he has na the waap a' the airm that my son has. I bred 'm, ye see, tae ,mv am n trade—a tailor—first, an' that's whaur he got the fine oratorical wheep o' the elbow. Mr, Agg Gardner has brought in a bill compel- ling every owner of a house above a certain height to provide a fire-escape where more than three families live on the premises. It is an excellent idea, but how is it Mr. Parnell's name is not on the back of the bill?

There is a fitness about the story of Aloltke's last game of whist which adds one more touch of com- pleteness to the great general's life. Playing his usual rubber on the night of his death,he won all 13 tricks—as complete a victory as he ever gained upon the field of battle. Ile now has all the honours, too.

The Princess of Wales, who is an experienced photographer, has sent a very large selection of her best productions to the great International Ex- hibition, which is to be opened next month at Vienna, under the patronage of the fashionable club of amateur photographers presided over by the Archduchess Maria Theresa.

Mr. Harford who was born at Bristol in 183 S. was apprenticed to the confectionery trade, but left it to work on the railway. He soon rose from being a porter to be a shunter, signalman, gnard, and in- spector, and when he had attained that comfortable position, accepted a requisition from his fellow rail- way servants to become district organising secret- ary. Railway companies are well represented in Parliament, and if Mr. Harford is returned he will be a tit representative of the men.

Mr. Edward Harford, secretary of the Amalgam- ated Society of Engineers and chairman of the Trade Union Parliamentary Committee, has been ' unanimously selected as a labour candidate by the Blackburn Liberal Association, and will at an early date be introduced to the constituency. Mr. Har- ford is a veteran trade unionist. Since 1873 he has served the Railway Men's Union, and has done great seivice to the cause of unionism. His recent action in Wales and Scotland on behalf of the men need not be recalled.

Mr. Poultney Bigelow, in his second article in the " Speaker" on Germany without Bismarck, after pointing out that Bismarck's strength in Germany has been not that he represented a party, a consti- tutional principle, or even a group of politicians but that he has been, and represents to-day, the, negation of popular government, says that "Bis- marck's twelve months of private life have been devoted to placing embarrassments in the path of Caprivi and in seeking to weaken the personal in- fluence of the Emperor."

More Ibsen. His portrait from a French source: —A collar of white beard, an aureola of white hair round a head of great power; a little man who takes short steps; speaks little, but thinks a lot; has been a druggist—hence in all his pieces there is some disease or other. He has been an actor— hence he will never consent to any cutting up of any Dart. Has been hissed in his own country— hence he lives abroad--mostly at Munich and Rome. I He knows no greater pleasure than sitting in a cafe for hours without saying a word to anyone.

Great changes are in contemplation in connection with the Wesleyan Missionary secretariat. It has been known for some months past that the Rev. Marmaduke C. Osborn would retire; and, unex- pectedly, the senior secretary, the Rev. John Wal- ton, who three years ago, at the urgent request of the Committee, took the place of the late Dr. Kilner, has now tendered his resignation, mainly on the ground that he has no longer the strength which the post demands. This has placed the General Committee in a dilemma.

Mrs. Grimwood, whose husband was one of the unfortunate victims of the Manipur disaster, is en- titled to rank amongst our nineteenth century I heroines. Her conduct on the night of the mas- sacre, during the retreat from Manipur,was charac- terised .with pluck and determination, while we learn that her knowledge of the country was invalu': , able in directing the party Here is indeed a sad I ending to a brief married life; for it is only three years since her husband, the Political Agent at Manipur, took her as a bride from England.

The women's question is to be raised in Parlia- ment not only by Mr. W oodall's Women's Suffrage Bill, but also on a resolution of which notice has been given by Professor Stuart, "That in the opinion of this House the law ought to be so altered asito enable women to be elccted on and to serve on county councils." The subject has not beenldirectly raised—except in the law courts—since the debates on the Scotch Local Government Bill, when the 1 Government resisted all overtures to admit women 1 to Scotch council boards, and this is a branch which I undoubtedly obtains a good deal of sympathy.

-- The lapse of a day or two can hardly be said to have had much effect on the "dissolution scare" created by the Education proposals of the Govern- ment. The probabilities of a general elecrion have been freely and even eagerly discussed by persons holding positions of the highest responsibility, , . I have not heard of a single sceptic in official quarters on either side, though some of the rank and file may be harder to convince. Amongst those who have sent messages to their local agents warning them to be on the alert are, to my know- ledge, several of the occupants of the Treasury bench.

-- It may be taken as a sign of the status attained by trade unions that the "Women's. Protective and Provident League" has now boldly changed its title to "The Women's Trade Union League." The League, which has its headquarters in London, was founded'in 1874 by a working woman, Emma Pater- son, and though it can hardly be said as yet to have achieved any signal success in the direction of , improving the conditions of women's labour, it has at least kept alive among working women the. idea of combination for purposes of defence and protec- tion. Some of the larger provincial unions, which are in a far more flourishing condition than the London societies,-have recently affiliated themselves to the League.

There are few worse records than that of the 1 Senapati, or Commander-in-Chief-, of Manipur, of whom Indian telegrams have recently said so much. Ills name, as we have before informed our readers, Is Tikendrajit Singh, and he is a step-brother of the overthrown Maharajah. his popular name, " Koi- reng," means the Wanderer. Our Calcutta contem- porary," The Englishman," says: Four years ago Koireng was found guilty of an atrocious murder, and was exiled to Lake Loktak for a year by Colonel Johnstone. More recently he wreaked his vengeance upon two villagers for a fancied offence by placing them on a mechan and lighting a fire below them. I For half roasting these poor wretches Koireng was I only fined fifty rupees.

-- It is strange that the two men who in recent years have made the strongest stand against the advancing tide of unionism should both have died on the same evening, Mr. John Walker, of the North British Railway, and Mr. Norwood, of the Joint Docks Committee in London, both of whom ' were engaged, in lighting against John Burns. There was another coincidence in the circumstance that at Waterloo Station,where Mr. Walker expired, there sbr.-AA hm:i been 111 llttOld,"c thf.i prQsent 1. • A,— .._. b - . and the immediately past genera-1 , wintigiere (it: the South-Western, one of whom was named Schott and the other Scotter. The scene at Waterloo, lam told \ by an eyewitness, was most affecting,the old friends and colleagues of Mr. Walker being unable to restrain their tears.

Yet another expedition to Mashonaland ! Lord Randolph, it seems, is not to have the "Land of Ophir" all to himself. General Booth has just des- patched a search party from the Cape to hunt, though not for lions or gold. The expedition con- sists of six men and a boy, the latter of native growth ; a Kimberley captain has been promoted per cable to the post of " major " and leader of the party, and the expedition has started with but few accoutrements. To be exact,it will boast one wagon, sixteen oxen, two horses, a tent, and for each man a /Vie. This last etcetera is quite a novelty for an army corps, but it is provided in order to obtain feathered luxuries,and because the lions of the land may be unacquainted with S.A. soldiers, and may fail to distinguish them from common explorers. Lord Randolph would indeed be surprised should he encounter the "Blood and Fire" contingent dur- ing his " up-country " travels.

But never trust 'em fur' no yo' con throw a bull bi th' tail. ' Ther's chaps as poo's long faces, an' quotes Scripter o ther lives. But dosen'd treeat like Kristians ther childer an' ther wives ; An' them as.lets 'em werk an' clam till they gooa suppin' ale, A w'd ne'er trust them fur' nor aw could throw a bull bi th' tail. A HOSS OV ANOTHER COLOUR. This sayin' hes nowt to do wi hosses, nor th' colour o' hosses ; it's summat like sayin', "There's two sides to a ladder," or "One tale's good till another's towd." If yo' want a illustrashun, here's one in a true tale abeawt a lawyer an' a butcher, as booath livPd i' Lancashire. Yo' see this butcher, like mony moor foos as there is, thowt he could ged th' best of a lawyer ! Sooa he went to th' lawyer's offis an' towd his tale :—" Ali name's Sooa-an'-Sooa, an' aw'm a butcher, an' last Setterda' a dog coon' into th' shop un' collared a leg o' Mutton off th' stock, an' wod aw want to know is iv th' dog's owner con be med to pay for th' leg o' mutton as his dog stooale." "Oh, certainly, certainly," said th' lawyer ; "whose dog was it." "ID WER Yon's !" Neaw,mony a chap as isn'd a lawyer wod ha'done a bit o' record cossin' at thad, but this lawyer dudn'd ; he took a pinch o' snuff, an' smiled quite sweet, an' then he axt th' butcher: "What's the damage ?" "Five bob," said th' butcher. "Well, then, you will owe me one-an-eight." "Owe tha one-an'-eight! Heaw the hangment dusta mek thad eawt ?" "how do I make it out ?" axt th' lawyer. "Why, there's six-and-eight Pence for my advice, less five shillings the price of the leg of mutton, leaving one- and-eight due to me." Thad butcher paid th' brass; 'sooa yo' see as wod he thowt wer a hoes ov another colour torned eawt to be a hose o' quite another colour still. A STITCH IN TIME SAVES NINE. Sometimes this sayin's used at th' wrang time: yo've 'happen bin tellin' a funny soeart o' ehap as yo've bin upset aboawt a stitch as hes bothered yo' a goodish bit latly, an' Meted o' sayin' heaw ill-off he wor he's grinned i' yo'r face, an' dug yo' i'th' ribs, an' said: " Ne'er mind, owd cock !" A stitch i' time saves nine,' tha knows." Seven days wi' herd labour is a lot too good for sich chaps as these. THERE'S NOWT LIKE LEATHER. This is a lie to begin wi', becos mooast o' th' Kesmas geese as aw've hed hes bin just like leather, an aw think as other fooak 'll say th' same abeawt th' geese they've bed. Yo' see ther's sich a demand for these animals at Kesmas (aw dorn'd know wod for) they con pass owt off, an' it's a rare thing for th' doctor as id is sooa. 'Appen they pay th' goose sellers a trifle on ev'ry toff goose they sell. Aw'd welly forgetten to menshun another thing as is welly like leather, an' that's another animal co'd beet; id runs th' geese a clooase race, am' th' wost on't is it's i' season an' sowd o' th' year reawnd. ITS NE'ER TO LATE TO MEND.. Aw hecn'd mich to say ageean this when it's applied to human bein's, but when id isn'd, an' it's meant to bring in ev'rything, aw say, " Yigh id is !: Wod abeawt boots as is worn to th' far eat?" Wi' this eksepshun aw say : Yo' may ha: spent thad mich i' drink Till yo've no moor to spend' An' then yo'll 'appen stop an' think It's ne'er to late to mend.
Yo'r temper may ha' med yo' foes, An' lost yo' mommy a friend; Then id may strike yo', 'mong yo'r woes,. It's ne'er to late to mend.

But my advice is do-nod wait Till yo' ged to th' far end, • An' iv yo' meean i ged agate— It's ne'er to late to mend. FOORCED MED'SUN-S GOOD FOR MAD DOGS. This is varra true,. 'speshly iv th' foorced med'- sun's a dose o' bullets o' lead wi' a hofe an' eawnee o' gunpeawder to bazk id up; aw wer ne'er one as wer i' favour o' dogs bein' alleawed to roam abeawt when they wer mad.. It's just th' • same wi' fooak, for yo'll mooatis aa chaps as tries to thump th' poleecemen geds some fooarced med'sun shape ov a tooathri cracks o'th' heyd wi' a trunshon, fol- lowed bi seven days, herd labour. Or 'appen a young chap goons offerin' to mek up to another young chap's th' young chap gi's him a good Ov coourse id does 'em a lot o' good. A LAME TILE. We o' mek game Ov a chap 'at's lame Whim he enters for a race. An' we do just same Wi' a tale lame As soon as id shows id face.

We know a fib , When we see id jib, . No matter 1' wod disguise; An' th' chap's a foo' As corn'd see through Lame tales, excuses, an' lies. NEET BRINGS TH' CROWS HOOAM. Nod okz, id doesn'd ; it's °Mier mornin' side as brings 'em hooam, an' mony a time it's the Bobby— iv th' crow hes enough brass abeawt him to tip th' Bobby Wl'. Th' habits o' th' crows bas awtered ' aboon a bit She aw were a lad, an' they hey'nd awter'd for th' better, let me tell yo'. But theer,aw dolled want to preych a sermon; it's appen summat like th' tale as a mate o mine tells abeawt a fayther tawkin to his son. Th' fayther were hlowin' th' lad up for stoppin' eawt late ov a neet, an> he finisht up wi' this argyment— " When ato wet a lad, my fayther med me be V the house an' 1 bed bi hofe-past !Anis ev'ry fleet." " Ay, a nice fayther ye' hed," said the lad, impi- dently. " Aw'll let tba know," th' lad's fayther said: " aw'll let tha know as aw'd a dal'd seet better fay- ther nor ever tha hed, tha impideqt young monkey !" An' th' impident young monkey laft harder than ever, SWEEP ABEAWT Till OWN DOORSTEP. A bit moor gradely good advice, an' it's a pity id isn'd olez acted on, for aw'm sooary to say as varra few wimmen wears eawt mony brushes i' indulgin' i' this healthy pastime; they seem to prefer Chad onhealthier pastime o' throwin' nasty waiter on ther nebburs' doorsteps. Aw know as this bit's herd to mek eawt, but ther's a tooathri fooak as con undo 0, knot, an, among 'em is these :- 1 Muttin, fooals as cQ't3 yttlq fooo for stuttiu', Doctori4 AS gi's attacks bad nameS, Nooipaper chaps as co' one another ignorant, Paysons as fo's eawt wi' th' Salvayshun Army, Teetotal speawter as pitches into publicans, An' lastly, o' sooarts o' hypocrites an' liars.

div.head: MR. PARNELL AT CLONMEL.
div.p: MR. PARNELL AT CLONMEL.

. . Mr. Parnell replying to a vote of confidence at Clon- mel, on Sunday, said he had a perfectly clear conscience regarding the evicted tenants, and had always been op- posed to the Plan of Campaign. He doubted its policy and practicability, and felt sure it would end in difficul- ties. He never desired to make capital out of the evicted tenants, and was at present responsible to the bank for an overdraft in supporting them. Mr. Parnell has re- plied to Mr. Justin M'Carthy's letter regarding the evicted tenants. He denies that he ever made the pro- mise alleged. -A6--

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 2, 1891. THE TRADES OF WARRINGTON. 1 PER C IVAL., GOR D 0 N ;
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 2, 1891. THE TRADES OF WARRINGTON. 1 PER C IVAL., GOR D 0 N ;

INTERESTING INFORMATION. Evidence of a very interesting character as to the industries of Warrington was given last week (as briefly reported in our last issue) by Mr. George Woods and Mr. R. A. Naylor, before the House of Commons Committee which is dealing with the proposed Lancashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Railway Bill. In answer to the inquiries of Mr.. Pembrol-e, 11-. Woods mentioned that there were five firms in Warrington connected with the wire-drawing industry, and in fact Warrington was the seat of the wire - drawing industry of England. The firm with which he was connected (the Longford Wire Company) em- ployed about 150 hands, but two larger works employed about 500 or 600 each. His own firm. made about 100 tons of wire a week, and they were large makers of wire mattresses and railway carri- age seats. The iron trade of Warrington was very large. He should say that the amount of wire rods made in Warrington, that was to say, rods out of which wire was made, would average about 70,000 tons per annum ; and the amount of wire made would be about 50,000 tons per annum. One of the concerns in Warrington engaged in the iron indus- try, had a capital of £1,000,000, £BOO,OOO, paid up, and consumed, or did consume, about 160,000 'tons of coal per annum, and made about 100,000 tons of bars and sheets. The total amount of bars and sheets made at Warrington in the year would be about 150,000 tons, and of pig iron consumed about 170,000 tons. lie was of opinion that the number of hands employed in the wire, iron, and steel industries, including engineers, file cutters, &P., of Warrington was between 5,000 and 6,000. The total consumption of coal in Warrington in the year would be about 450,000 tons. .As a matter of opinion, Air. Woods did not think the Derbyshire coalfields would be able to compete at Warrington with the coallieLls of South Lancashire, but he knew that when necessity had arisen, during disturbances. there was a very large amount of coal brought from the neighbourhood of Chesterfield and from South Yorkshire. As to the manufacture of wire netting, Mr. Woods declared that more netting was made at Norwich than at any other place in the world, but Warrington came next. Questioned as to the other industries of Warrington Mr. Woods pointed out that there was a manufacture daily becoming more important, that of gas-stoves, for the making of which there was one large manufactory and another just commenced. That was a branch of industry which was capable of large extension by means of railway facilities. Then they had two cotton factories in Warrington ; one employing about 1,000 hands and the other 200 hands. In the making of fustian, Warrington was a very import-- ant centre, and, furthermore, the town had twelve tanneries, the annual value of the leather made being about £250,000. Connected with that he be- lieved all the tanning material called shumac was brought from the Continent via Hull and Grimsby to Warrington. There were two very important glass works in Warrington, employing between them 300 and 400 hands, and yearly turning out about £90,000 worth of the better qualities of glass. Amongst the other important works in Warrington enumerated by Mr. Woods, were soap works with an output of between 150 and 200 tons a week; breweries which were said to send out about 500,000 barrels a year; two important cabinet works; lead works; a very large flour mill; and other places sending out about 500,000 tons of galvanised iron in the year. In addition to all these they had the most important manufactory of files in the world— Peter Stubbs's. Altogether the total tonnage of Warring,ton in and out was calculated to be about 1,200,000 tons per annum. Mr. R. A. Naylor's evidence was chiefly confined to the timber trade in which he is engaged. He said that he shipped large quantities of timber from Liverpool, Garston, West Hartlepool, Mull, and Grimsby direct to the consumers, but he also brought large quantities to Warrington for manu- facturing purposes as well as for local consumption. They made everything that was required in the construction of a building, such as doors, windows, and staircases, and the like. They also had a large turning business for the purpose of supplying brush manufacturers in different parts of the country.. In addition to the sea-borne trade they had rather an extensive trade in home-grown timber, the main supply of which was got from Cheshire la_ut some from Wales and some from Ireland. It wAhl be a great advantage to be put in communication with the Nottingham forests, because the timber round Warrington was becoming very scarce—the chemi- cal vapours had destroyed a great quantity. If the new line was opened cat it would be a great °Avail- t-,age to the timber trade of W arrington.

div.head: Tr E REGINIENT.
div.p: Tr E REGINIENT.
DY SYLVANUS COM.
CHAPTER IX.

THE MOTHERS—A' RETROTHMENT. In the extreme western corner of Dorsetehire, ()lose upon the Devon border, was located the broad manor of Elmdale. The greater part of the estate was of a wild and mountainous character, but a source of wealth, nevertheless, the rugged hills abounding in quarries whence came the best building marble of the realm. There were beauti- ful, verdant stretches, however, on which were productive farms, and in the rich valleys fruit grew and perfected with but little fostering. The estate took its name, probably, from the demesne of its lord, the inanor-house being situated in a wide, romantic dale, bounded by verdant hills, where grew in abundance some of the finest elms in the kingdom. The mansion was a large Gothic structure, built mostly of native marble, surrounded by parks and gardens and prolific preserves, all laid out with artistic taste and, shille and kept in the best manner. On a dull, lowery afternoon of the last day of September, Roland Archer paced to and fro on the broad piazza that extended the whole length of the front of the mansion. He wee twenty-seven years of age,.of 'medium height, stoutly and rather clumsily framed; dark of complexion, with coarse black hair, and a pair of sombre, restless eyes. His brow was full and bread, and wonderfully furrowed for one of his yeers • the nose long and thin; lips thin and hard and pale ; the chin receding, both chin and lower jaw lacking manly prominence. He was habited in the garb of a country gentleman, of rich, costly material, and, notwithstanding the state of the weather,. he carried his cocked hat in his hand. Examined. critically, Roland Archer. was not such a man as one would choose for a bosom friend, yet he was gentlemanly-looking, and by many might have been called handsome, but never so called by one of • pure heart and tender affection. Never would he have been deemed even manly looking by the maiden who sought faith and love and warm devotion. Thus paced the man to and fro, raising his head, ever and anon, and sweeping with his eyes the beautiful expanse that lay spread out before him,. murmuring, as he gazed, of pomp and power within his grasp, when, from a small door, or wicket, by the side of the grand portal, came forth a man to join him—a middle-aged mane, wearing se wig ; his ferret-like eyes gleaming be- hind a pair of iron-bowed spectacles a his features sharp and prominent, with skin like parchment;. haleited in the garb of an attorney-at-law, and, carrying in his hand a bundle of papers. "Well, Bowles," said Archer, stopping in his. walk as the attorney came up, and putting on his, hat, "how do you, find it?' is all clear?' "As clear as daylight, my lord. There is no- question anywhere which we could not answer— aye, and truly answer. As for your title, that the Lord High Chancellor has himself decreed, as he was in duty bound to do." "My brother's title he decreed," corrected Rce land, with a twitching of the facielemuscles which, he could not prevent. "Bless us! and isn't that the same ateyour own,, my lord? If your brother was true Earl of Elmdale when he died, you must be just as truly earl now; and, furthermore, there is nothing to interfere with your full and unhampered possession. Richard never had a son, and his only child, an infant daughter, died when he did. The coronet is yours, beyond any power in the United Kingdom to wrest. it from you. That' you know. And now, with regard to the condition of the estate, I= find every- thing eminently, satisfactorily. The bounds are, clearly defined; the tenants are of the very best- class ; the quarries are worked faithfully, and are. yielding a princely revenue. Your lordship is to be congratulated.. There is not a fairer possession in, Dorsetshire." And yet Roland Archer shook his head. Thera was wondrous music in the lordly title as it fell from the lawyer's lips, and the fact of succession, was clear enough, but not yet was- he the respon- sible lord of the domain. The Court of Chancery had promulgated a decree in favour of Richard Archer, and the chancellor was- straining every nerve to find him. To Roland it seemed that not more effort eould have been put forth to find a lost monarch. But—would they find him?' The younger brother had learned by. heart a certain passage in the last letter he had received from. dear old Dick." It-bore date in July—aboutthe- middle—but the writer had not been permitted, to- tell where he was. "ROLAND, DRY BROTHER, for the love of Heaven, do not delay. My captors spare neither sex nor age. If my ransom is not forthcom- ing very soon, both my darling and myself must, die,, and our poor old Nancy,with,us. Fo7get it not-0.1 lovet it not !—your brother's life is in your hands !" And this Roland Archer had repeated to himself hundreds of times, and yet he had not lifted a. fin- ger towards saving his unfortunate kindred. To those who asked him concerning Sir Richard he simply answered: "Since the death of his wile he has been like one bereft. His last letter gave me information that he had planned to return home by way. of, the Alps and Switzerland." Later, he added to the story. He said he. had received a letter from a friend of his brother. in Rome, informing him that Richard had been attacked on the highway by mountain ba,nditti,and that the whole party had been slain. And he ex- hibited a letter, soiled and worn, bearing the post- marks of Toulon and. Paris; but the postmarks had been made with a pen, and the paper was of English manufacture. So those who had known Sir Richard mourned his death in, sorrow deer. and sincere: and the /pore 6ofrow was there that ItOlEaCti instead ot Richard, was to be Earl of Elmdale.. "You speak truly, Bowles," the expectant heir at length returned to the last remark of his com- panion. "I know the title is lear,, without a flaw, and I shall be greatly relieved when the whole business is settled. Heaven; knows I would surrender every hope of wealth and titled honour if thereby I could bring old Dick home, safe and well; but alas!' if he is really dead I wish the court could know it." " I think you are very soon trehe relieved," said the attorney, with an assuring nod. "The ehana eellor has sent direct to our commander-in-chief lia, Spain—so Laos credibly inforreed—sad we may be' sure that in the English army, somewhere will be found a man who will furnish the information. Sir. Arthur's corresponding secretaries are in command- cation with all parts of the continent, and we may believe that the robbery and murder of so Reveille neat a man as you brothee cannot be lons_leepe from the publib. Yes, Sir Arthur will be Tare to answer. If Richard is, perchance, alive and held captive—All 1 What is it!; What startled you. seo?" "Nothing, nothing," gasped the lstiveriing wretch. "Yet," he added, atter a briefe straggle for self-control. "I believe your words ava startle me. I never thought of it before, but yeue reenark caused to flash upon my mind a possibility el,' dear Dick's captivity among those murderceres beaditti. I have heard of their holding prisoncenefor exorbi- tant ransoms, and cruelly hutcherinlstheze if the ransoms were not forthcoming." "My lord," responded Bowles., with ranch show of feeling, "you must not borrow, trouble in that direction. If Richard had heen held. captive to ransom by the banditti, you, of all leen in the world, would have received the first, intelligence, for to you they vzould have loohnd fee the money. I know how they/ do these thirscr. No, no; your not having receevell your brother'a call for aid is, proof positive that-he is not held, captive by the, banditti." Roland wae,foreed to take a. bun towards a Zee part of the piazza to hide a laok ef conscious gailt which he kaaw must manifeat heat. As he turned to retrace bin steps his attention was ettracted.ley an exclamation of the atherneye and on follewing the direction of the latter's gaze., he saw a heavy travelling carriage coming %se the path lawn the highway. Why, he was frightened heacould not have told; yet a. mortal terror seized hint' 1, and a cog,. clammy sweat stood upon his brow. The carriage was driven to the foot of the broad marble steps, and, these !stopped, when a valet, who had been seated witelathe drivee„ alighted, and threw open the anor. The first to alight was a men: whom Roland secognized at, once—Sir Edmund Cooper—a well- to-do baroneak, whosesplace was, across the border in Devonshire, near the princely. estate of the Earl of Oxton. "I remember him very well,' nodded Elmdalee "Well, my lord, there is likely to transpire a ise more wonderful case of unexpected succession to that grand old title and estate than was that through which you same to this inheritance. The present Earl of Oxton is Walter Buckley : and be is , the seventh of the line, he having come to the title ,in seventeereninety-feew,„ l'ho titie_wamNeted tA.

div.head: HIGH LEGH CHURCH ON FIRE.
div.p: HIGH LEGH CHURCH ON FIRE.

COMPLETE DESTRUCTION. On Saturday morning St. John's Church, High Leah, was destroyed by fire. The church had been undergoing decoration and it is thought that on Friday night, shortly after nine o'clock, when the lamps were extinguished by the workmen, previous to leaving the church, a piece of wick tell, un- noticed, upon some painters' cloths lying, beneath. These, after smouldering for some hours. 4there is evidence that the church was safe at two, o'clock in the morning), must ultimately have buret into that flame which ended in the complete destruction of the building. About half-past four iothe morning, Mr. John Cbolc, churcbwarden, got up; and saw the fire, flames from which found their. way into his yard. Quickly he gave the alarm, and his son went off on horseback to summon the members of the local fire brigade. They arrived too late to save the church, which was soon reduced to ruins, but suc- ceeded in preventing the spread of the flames to the neighbouring farm buildings. The church itself was insured by the Manchester Fire Office Company. There will, however, be a loss on the organ. a hand- some oak altar, and two altar cloths, valued altoge- ther at several hundred pounds„ Fortunately„ all the registers and other papers had been removed, for safety to the Vicarage, while the church was be- ing decorated, and they were, therefore, saved. The The Vicar (Rev, H. A. D. Surridge) at once made ar- rangements for re-building. A temporary church is being erected for use during the next few months. The Bishop of Chester has written a kind Wtter of sympathy to the Vicar, in which he expresses ap- proval of the course he has taken. In 3,889, the seats were re-arranged, an organ chamber added, and the whole building thoroughly restored. It was intended to decorate the interior after the Italian style. The workmen were engaged in decorating the ceiling and walls, and an artist, Mr, G. Hiller, was engaged in painting some figures of remarkable beauty on the walls. The interior of the church had probably never looked so well as on the eve of the fire. The destruction of the church is complete, as the building has been completely gutted. The church was built, as a Latin inscription over the doorway tells, as a thanksgiving for peace, after the battle of Waterloo, and was consecrated and endowed in 1816. According to a tradition which lingers hmong the old inhabitants, it was built on the site of a black and white Cheshire church, which the inscription above mentioned states was built in the year 1408. An old will of 1306 leave to the chaplain of Thomas de Legh, of the West Hall, the sum of sixpence, and as there was a chaplain, it may reasonably be supposed that there was also a chapel in existence. Orrnerod says, "A church existed at High Leah at the time of the conquest. Here is now a chappel of ease in this township, called High Leah chappel, within the parish of Rosthorn, which was built by Thomas Leah, of High Leah de East Hall, esquire, anno domini 1581, as I find the year, his name and coat of arms engraven in the stone on the side of the same chappell, in which every year his grandson, Geo. Legh, married Elizabeth, second daughter of Peter Leycester, of Nether Tabley, esquire." " Here was also another ancient chappell of ease in this township, belonging to the family of the Leghs, of the West Hall, .in High Leah. The fabric is yet standing nea to his house, but now converted to 'other uses by the heirs of the family. This chappel was built about the reign of Henry the Fourth."

div.head: LIBERAL BAZAAR CONCERT.
div.p: LIBERAL BAZAAR CONCERT.

The third concert in aid of the fund for the- bazaar in connection with the Warrington Liberal Association was held at the Liberal Club, Bewsey- st., on Monday evening, Mr. Thomas Morris,F,G.S., presided. There was a large attendance. The Chairman said that at the last concert whea their friend Councillor Pierpoint was in the chair he referred to the loss- which the club had sustained through the deaths of some of its best supporters Since the club had seen the worst, however, it had never looked behind it, but had kept going on towards the best; and he felt sure that eventually success would crown the efforts of the Committee, and that the club would soon be one of the happiest and most successful clubs which had existedin War- rington for many. years. (Applause.) lie hoped that might be so. There was every reason to believe that the concerts would be successful judging from the large attendance that evening • and he hoped the bazaar would be so likewise. All liberal-minded men who had the cause at heart would be pleased to know that Liberalism had such a backbone as the Liberal Club and that it was doing well,not with the assistance of, men who could afford all sorts of sums, but through that of horny-handed work- men. He believed the club would do well as long as it had such men connected with it. (Applause.)— The first piece was a quartette, (oboe, violin, viola, and violincello) Mozart, by Messrs. Ward, Caldwell, Johnson and Whitehead, who also in admirable style, contributed two other selections from Mozart during the-evening.. Mr. Paul Conway was heartily encored for his-song "The Diver," and gave,in compliance " The song that reached my heart." Mr. George Parr gave much satisfaction by his rendering of a song composed by Mr. E. Whitehead, the leader of the, quartette party, "Old Ireland shall blossom again," And in response to an enthusiastic encore, repeated the last verse. Messrs: Conway and Parr fol- lowed with the duet" Excelsior," this concluding the first part of theprogramme. THU RSD AY . On Thursday, Mr. Noble, the general manager of the Midland Railway, who was recalled, said there were 15 departures an hour from the Central Station in this city, and that certain parts of the line just outside were very crowded. Mr. Bidder, Q.C., submitted, for the Mid- land Company, that the new line would not pay, and that it would merely facilitate the transit of coal to a few places and help gouty people to get to Buxton. On behalf of the London and North-Western Railway Company, Mr. Littler, Q.C., addressed the Com- mittee in a similar strain, and said there was nothing more injurious to the general rail- way service than to have insolvent lines dotted over the country. Mr. George Findlay the general manager of the London and North-Western Railway strongly objected to the proposed junction at Cheadle. and also tothe new company running into the Central Station. An extension of either the London-road Station or the Central Station was, he asserted, now practically impossible, and they were not by any means toe large for the accommodation of the probable future traffic. The flow of traffic, he said, as from north to south, and he did not think the line was likely to pay, for it would be costly in construction and would not gather up the traffic. The project was a great one, but there was neither head nor tail to it. Asked by Mr. Littler if he thought the line would be useful for strategic pur- poses, Mr. Findlay said, amid laughter, that he was the reader the other day of a paper on "Strategic Railways," but really the proposed new line never occurred to him.

200 NATIVES KILLED. A Reuter's telegram reports that on the morning of the 25th General Graham's column (which started from ramu for Manipur) attacked one thousand of the enemy, entrenched in earthworks. Severe hand-to.hand fighting followed, and the enemy was routed with the loss of two hundred men. On the British side one native officer was killed, and Lieutenant Grant and other officers were wounded. A telegram from Simla says :—On the morning of the 25th inst., General Graham discovered 1,000 of the enemy, who occupied some earthworks, surrounded by a marsh. Their only way of retreat being cut off, the troops ad- vanced to the position. Severe hand-hand-hand fighting ensued, resulting in the rout of the enemy, who lost 200 men. On the British side one native officer was killed, whilst Captain Drury and Lieutenants Grant, Cox, and Carnegy were wounded.
_ THE SUCCESS OF THE EXPEDITION. ROUT OF THE ENEMY. OCCUPATION OF THE CAPITAL.

A Renter's telegram, dated Manipur, via Kaireng, Monday, states :—The Kohima, Cachar, and Tanu columns all reached this place yesterday, the march of all three expeditions having been conducted in admirable .accord with the dispositions of the Indian military authorities. The aspect of the place when the British 'forces, after their long march, at length reached the re- mote town which was so lately the scene of warfare and el;ataghter was extraordinary. Scarcely a single human being was to be seen. The whole capital was wrapped in silence. As the trogps marched in the midst of the elusiers of houses they -encountered rio enemy, for there , was not a fighting man within the walls. It was a deserted city. Moving ,on warily, the British force entered the enclosures of the palace of the Maharajah. Hare also was absolute stillness. All the occupants had fled. The magazine had been blown up and the interior of the palace was a wreck. It had been sacked fromendto end, hardly a thing of value remaining with- in it. One discovery which 4 though not unexpected, sent a thrill of horror through all the ranks were made. Within the Palace enclosure were found the heads of the British officials and officers who had fallen a prey to the treachery of the rulers of Manipur. The Rajah, the Sena- putty, and the Princes had escaped the vengeance which they feared, having' as it was soon learned, fled from the town some time before the arrival of the British, tak- ing a north-easterly direction,the only open road of escape The greetings between the three British columns were hearty. From first to last the Kohima and Cachar de- tachments met with no resistance,but the Tamu column had a fight near Thobal. The Manipur army seems to have concentrated there. They had taken up an intrenched position, bounded an both sides by swamps,in which the troops could not operate. A reconnaissance having in- formed the General of the position of affairs, he detached , a body of troops to cut off the only line of retreat, and , then attacked the enemy's position in front. The Mani- puns defended their earth-works obstinately, and there as hand-to-hand fighting in the trenches as the British 'tmops poured into them. But there was soon a total mut, and the position was in the hands of General Gra- ham. One hundred and ninety of the enemy fell,among the killed being two officers, whom their dress distin- &shed as being of high rank, RETURN OF BRITISH TROOPS. Manna?, TUESDAY.—No news has yet been received here of the Maharajah, the Senaputty, or other princes. Ninety wen of the mounted infantry started in pursuit this morning. A committee of officers has exhumed the bodies cf the victims fo-day. The funeral service over the remains will be held on the 30th inst. A committee has been appointed to inquire into the recent events in Manipur. Some of the troops will begin returning to India and Burtnah at once. Scarcity of food prevails in the country owing to the people near Manipur having fled at the approach of British troops. :-.ireneral Collett is now, however, restoring confidence.

div.p: THE NEW LOCAL RAILWAY.

The. Select Committee of the House of Commons, presided over by Mr. Walter James, sat again on Monday, and heard further evidence in support of this Bill. Mr. R. Robinson was called. He said that he had had about 40 years', experience of railway traffic. For 26 years he was traffic miaager to the Great I Northern .Railway in the Yorkshire district, and I filled similar posts on otherlines. He believed that ' this line wouldeccommodate glarge and important district, from which it would receive considerable traffic. Beyond the plates Which the line itself touched, it mould shorten the distances from many places on other lines, notably from all places south of Newark to the Cheshire district. From Birken- head to Chesterfield by the proposed line and the Cheshire lines it would be 84 miles, whereas the routes by the existing railways ranged from 92 miles to 111 miles. Witness put in a time table showing the train service and the timenow occupied on the journey by existing railways between a number of places compared with the time which would be occupied en the journey by the new line. From Chesterfield to Newark the new line would Shorten the journey by 13 miles, and save 1 hour 8 minutes in time. . From Chesterfield to Lincoln there would be a shorter journey by 21 miles, and a saving of time of 11 hours. The table contained a number of-similar calcula- tions. The witness pointed out that these facts would, of course, influence the railway rates. He next put in a table showing the comparative traffic earnings and cost of construction per mile on the paid up capital of a num- ber of the principal railway companies of England and Wales. The average revenue on the gross receipts per mile in work for the year 1889 was £4879, and the aver- age cost per mile on the paid up capital for the year 1889 was £51,000. In regard to the proposed line requiring a gross-revenue of £425,000 to , pay 4 per cent., £2,640 would be a sufficient revenue on -the gross receipts per mile. On the capital of £5,0009000 the cost per mile worked ontat.£3l,lo4. The engineer's estimate of cost of lands and works of the new line was £4,227,522; the capital £5,000,000 over the length of railway, 1601 miles.—ln answer to further questions, witness said that he saw no reason why the trains of the proposed line should not conveniently run into the Central Sta- tion at Manchester. There .47AS qpthiag in the circumstances of the station to .pfevent such a thing. The new line would be of considerable value to the Great Eastern Railway, as by .a junction at Lincoln it would enable them to run into .a new district for them. At the present time, they were asking for permission for running powers over the whole of the line, but the pro- moters at present were only willing to.give these powers as far as Chesterfield.—Cross-erp,nined by Mr. Littler, Q.C. (for the.Manchester,Sheffielelyand Lincolnshire.)— He admitted that along a considerable portion of the proposed linelre.m.Warrington there was no large indus- try • but he pointed out that the ,railway would pass through and dev.elop a district from which a good traffic could be derived. The new railway would be able to carry coal frcun. Chesterfield to Warrington kr about half-a-crew.n a ton. He believed that the St. Helens rate was only 1041.4 but he thought that a traffic could never- theless be created. from Chesterfield. Witness was not aware that on some lines where the gradient was not more than lin .70 the working expenscs were ashigh as 70 percent. At this point theConunittee adjourned. TUESDAY.

div.head: -.,..-.. THE GOSPEL OF ST. JOHN.
div.p: -.,..-.. THE GOSPEL OF ST. JOHN.

Under pressure upon our space, the following argument on behalf of the genuineness of St. John's Gospel, was ommitted from Mr. Dignum's letter in our last issue : The force of the argument with respect to John's gos- pel especially, I think may be put in a light to bring the subject home to everyone, at once realistic and convinc- ing. Our modern theorists ask us to believe that this gospel was a forgery, imposed upon the churches about the middle of the 2nd century. Let us try to grasp the meaning of the situation at the time Irenteus wrote by a supposition founded upon the history of another John, the St. John of England as he has lately been called— the venerable Wesley. He died on the 2nd March, 1791. Now let us suppose that he had never written a book at all, or only an Epistle or two at most. At the time of his death his doctrines and teachings were known throughout the whole of Great Britain and Ireland, and in many parts of the continent of Europe and America. But between the year 1821 and 184 I—that is from 30 to 50 years after his death kcorresponding to the 30 to 50 years after the Apostle John's death)—a hitherto un- known book is foisted upon the Methodist Churches, teaching facts and doctrines utterly unknown to Wes- ley,and so early as between the years 1821 and 1841 pre- tended to be a production of-John Wesley himself. En- deavour now to realize the position. At that period there were living many eminent ministers who had been sent out by Wesley to promulgate his teachings, men who had often communed with himtlistened to his discourses, and knew all about the great facts and doctrines he taught; and we are to suppose it possible that these men actually accepted an outrageous forgery utterly opposed to their great leader's teaching, and that with- out s, note of protest being raised:! Not a word is heard from such witnesses as Clarke or Bunting or Lessey, or Newt= or Dixon or Waddy living about that time, or from the innumerable company of laymen dispersed in all parts who must have heard Wesley preach in their early manhood, and could readily test the new facts and doctrines of that book with what they had heard from hic own lips! Moreover we must suppose that some Methothst Irenteus, say the late Venerable George Osborn ,could have written a work about 1861, 70 years after Wesley's death, affirming that the strange book was certainly his and had always been received as such! Could absurdity go further? And yet this is precisely the relative position of things in the 2nd century with respect to,the Gospel of John, unless we admit as we are cdmpefisd-to do upon the testimony of Irenseus that it was the genuine production of the Apostle and corres- ponded with all his teachings.

THE AUDACIOUS ROBBERY FROII A
FARM LABOUR.ER.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Sat- urday, before Alderman Chandley (chairman), and Burgess,and Councillor Voisey, Thomas Farrell, was I brought up on remand charged with violently assault- ing and robbing, of 255., in the Higher Angel Inn, ' Buttermarket-St., on the previous Tuesday afternoon, James Cunningham, employed as a labourer by Mr. Edward Percy, of Field House Farm, near Widnes. Two other men named William Moran, and John Butler, had been charged with being concerned in , the affair, but were discharged. Mr. J. L. Whittle appeared for the prosecution. He stated that on the preceding Monday, the complainant, who is employed by Mr. Edward Percy, of Field House Farm, near Widnes, as a labourer, came from Fern- worth to Warrington, and slept at the lodging- house of John Farrell, the prisoner's father, in Hill- et. He had the 255. concealed in a watch fob cut from an old pair of trousers, and tied inside the front of his shirt. Mr. Whittle explained that the prisoner became aware that he had some money about him, and on the following day while they were drink- ing together in company with Moran and Butler rushed at him, and with a knife cut his shirt open and robbed him of the 2.55. The main facts of the case have been previously reported and were now re-detailed more at length by the complainant and his witnesses. The former stated that he treated the three men to several glasses each with some loose money he had about him, never opening the foie. They were all sober. On his being robbed by the prisoner he went to the tap room door and shouted go for the police," and the prisoner pulled him from the door, and then he fell under the table. He accused Moran of having the money, believ- ing the prisoner to have given him it.—Mr. Whittle said if the other prisoners had not been discharged, he ''could he thought, with the evidence he had, have brought a good case against them.—The prisoner who assumed quite an air of injured innocence, subjected the pro- secutor to a close examination.—Edith Susannah Critch- ley, daughter of the landlord of the Higher Angel, repeated her former evidence, and Emma Critchley, her sister, corroborated, and Police-sergant Taylor again de- posed to the circumstances of the prisoner's apprehension. In the struggle between Cunningham and the prisoner, both had their fingers cut with his knife, and Sergeant Taylor said he found in Farrell's coat pocket a piece of Cunningham's shirt, cut out by the prisoner, and stained with blood. The prisoner asserted that the Sergeant had failed to find this upon him after three searchings, and afterwards himself put it into the pocket of the coat, then produced it from the pocket. This Sergeant Tay- lor emphatically denied, and said he found the piece on the first search. The prisoner reserved his defence; and was committed for trial to the Liverpool Assizes.

div.head: CtIILIA.N WAR. INSURGENT IRONCLAD BLOWN UP. 200 LIVES LOST.
div.p: THE CtIILIA.N WAR. INSURGENT IRONCLAD BLOWN UP. 200 LIVES LOST.

SATURDAY.—The Ironclad Blanco Encalada, one on the most powerful war vessels held by the Con- gressionalists. was sunk in Caldera Bay on the 23rd inst., by Government torpedo boats. It is estimated that 200 of those on board perished. PARIS, SIINDAY.—The Chilian Legation here has received a telegram stating that the ironclad Blanco Encalada was destroyed by two torpedoes discharged from the Government cruiser Almirante Lynch, com- manded by Captain Fuentes. The Government torpedo flotilla was commanded by Captain Moraga. Among the bodies recovered of those who perished in the destruc- tion of the Blanco Encalada is that of Senor Barros Luco, one of the leaders of the Parliamentary party. PARIS, SUNDAY.—According to the particulars of the blowing up of the Blanco Escalada, received through the Chili= Congressional sources, the ironclad was moored to thnquay in Caldera Bay, when it was surprised by the torpedo boats, and only on the seventh attack did the latter succeed in destroying the vessel. Senior Valdez Verzona, the commodore, eight officers, and 150. men perished. A PITCHED RATTLE.—ROUT OF GOVERNMENT

div.head: TROOPS. ENORMOUS SLAUGHTER.
div.p: TROOPS. ENORMOUS SLAUGHTER.

NEW YORK, SATURDAY.—lntelligence has only just reached New York from Callao of a desperate battle which was fought between the Chilian Government troops and the insurgent forces at Pozo Almonte on the 7th of March. The insurgents at first had by far the' worst of the battle, and were driven back, leaving a num- ber of their men in the hands of the victors. Opportune reinforcements came up, however, and the insurgents, resuming the offensive, finally routed the Government troops of whom 500 were killed or wounded. The in- surgents purchased their victibry very dearly, for they lost 800 killed and wounded, exclusive of an unknown cumber of prisoners, who were barbarously shot by their captors on the retreat. The Government troops retired in fairly good order on Camina, destroying the nitrate works in the district as they passed.
te.cording to another dupatch received via Panama, and dated the 12th inst., a cablegram from Iquique had brought the news that the insurgents had taken posses- sion 4i Arica and Tacna unopposed.

THE CHARGE OF CAUSING THE DEATH
OF I WOMAN. INQUEST AND VERDICT.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday, Alfred Whittaker was brought up on remand charged with causing the death of Margaret Broom- head, aged 46, widow of Alonzo Broomhead, master builder, on the previous Sunday morning, and again remanded pending the coroner's inquest to be held that day. Tha inquest was held by Mr. S. Brighouse at the White Hart Inn, Sankey-st., on Saturday afternoon. Whittaker was present at the enquiry. The inquest was fixed for 12 but some of the jury coming from ten to fifteen minutes /ate, Inspector Spinks com- plained that jurymen in Warrington seemed to think they were paying a compliment to the police in coming to do her Majesty's work when warned by them to do so. They could not get them to come there ppnctually.—A juror: What do you call punctual ?—Another juror: I am almost sure he told me a quarter past 12.—A third juryman: He told me 12.—Inspector Spinks : They come very punctually in Latchford, because they are paid. —The Foreman.: Better try it on here.—The Coroner: A. very good reform: I am always in favour of jurymen being paid.—Robert Hugh Broomhead, aged 12, son of the deceased, repeated the evidence previously given at the Police Court, adducinc, some additional particulars. Witness and she were lodging at the house of John Howell, Whittaker's father-in-law, at 18 Portland-st.' and on Saturday night, she complained to witness that Mr. Howell had knocked her down, and she began carrying on, and then hit him across the cheek, upon which he
jumped up and pushed her against the table. Witness said" Do not touch my mother ; you are stronger than

_ her, and she is weak (she has ben on a bed of sickness. "She was quiet for awhile, then began again. A police-. man was sent for, but none could be found, and then Whittaker was brought, who said had become un: . .. . . _

bearable and must jo Out. he declined to do so, and he said if she dia not he would carry her out, and she ran back trying to get in. Whittaker took hold of her and witness and pushed them out, and she fell back against the curbstone, and cut her head. They went back presently to the front door and tried to get admis- sisn, but Mr. Howell said he would not have her in, and Whittaker begged him to let her come in. Mr. Howell said if she would be quiet and go to bed she could stop. They bathed her head, and she and witness went upstairs. When she got to the third stair from the top, she fell down on the back of her head again, and it bled. They bathed her head and carried her upstairs, and got her to bed. She never spoke again. When Mr. Whittaker pushed her out she was in the doorway trying to force her way in. It was not such a hard push. She was worse for drink.—By Inspector Spinks : Witness did not tell Inspector Cox,when he came,about the fall on the pavement, became ho was in so much trouble at the time. Pressed, on this point witness said he did not tell Inspector Cox because he had forgotten all about it.— The Coroner: Perhaps he was afraid, Mr. Spinks.— Witness in reply to Inspector Spinks, said the deceased in fallinc, downstairs fell past him and he tried to stop her, but had to jump over her to save himself. She fell backwards to the bottom of the stairs.—lnspector Spinks said the people in the house said they never heatd that fall. —Whittaker attempted to explain the circumstances as to the previous fall, when the Coroner told him he would have an opportunity of doing that after, if the jury wished to hear it, and if he had something to correct in the witness's statement.—The witness on being requested to sign his depositionse said he could not write the name.—ln reply to th Coroner he said he had learnt to read and write, but hist mother always told him to go in the name of Robert O'Neil, and he could write that, but not the name Rober- Broomhead.—Dr. John Turville Smith, senior house sur

geon at the Infirmary, deposed to the deceased being admitted there about half-past eight on Sunday night, the 19th. in a semi-conscious condition, and dyinc, there about 5.30 p.m. on the 22nd. He had, at the Coroner's request, made a post mortem examination. The body was that of a well-nourished woman. There was a lacerated wound on the scalp above and behind the right ear, and there were a few small bruises on the right arm, and one on the right shin. There was a linear fracture of the skull, extending to the base. Between the dura mater and the bone, at the corresponding point was a clot of blood. On the left side over the frontal lobe of the brain, and beneath the dura mater was a large clot of blood, with considerable laceration of the brain sub- stance. Both lungs were congested, and showed evi- dence of phthisis. The cause of death was pressure of the clot on the base of the brain, occasioned by the fracture of the skull. It was not possible to say whether the injuries were caused by the first fall or the fall downstairs. The fall that caused I them must have been a violent one. The fall. downstairs might have caused them.—The Coroner said although the fall in the street might have caused tle in juries, he did not see how the jury could come to that conclusion, frqm the evidence that they had, as in order to convict Whittaker properly, they must be satisfied that there wa„s no alternative cause, and supposing that ,it was his push that occasioned the fall which caused her death, there were the facts that the woman was drunk and noisy and would not go out of the house,upon which he pushed her, and that the boy himself said she was not pushed with any great amount of violence.—A juror re- marked that if, as was stated, he had hold of the boy with one hand and the deceased with the other, he could' not push her very hard.—The Coroner said all the sup-- positions were in favour of Whittaker. If there had been. no other fall, matters would have been far different. He was prepared to advise the jury that theywould be justi- dl,4 in returning ae,open verdict.—Thejury had a pri- vate ‘ileliberation for about ten minutes, and then re- corded a verdict that the deceased met her death through t clot on the base of the brain, caused by pressure of .• tee'skull, but whether the injury was the fracture o. caused by Alfred Whittaker, or by the deceased falling were unable to say, though they downstairs, the jur; were inclined to the lat.‘4l r conclusion.—The Coroner thin 't intimated to Whittaker thso far as that Court was con- ..

cerned, he was dischar-g. vain brought before the Whittaker was on Tuesday, a„., the verdict of the Warrington bench, but, owing „need by the police, `,l Coroner's jury, no evidence was adv„ • and he was accordingly discharged.

div.head: CLITHEROE CASE.
div.p: THE CLITHEROE CASE.
MR. JACKSON'S DEFENCE.

Mr. Jackson is about to issue a reply tolls wife's state- ment. A summary reply appears lathe "Northern Daily Telegraph." Mr. Jackson relates the whole of the strange eventful history of his courtship, repeated rejection, final acceptance, marriage on the following day, and depar- ture for New Zealand at once. He states that it was his wife who urged him to go away in face of his repeated offers to stay. Ile denies MN. Jackson's _statement as to the" h's ". remarking that his wife is too well educated to have needed correction. He went to New Zealand,not to buy land as Mrs. Jackson alleged, but to take up land which belonged to him, in consequence of his services in the Maori war. His application to his wife for money to return was, he says, in the nature of a joke, and his return was entirely due to his wife's repeated petitions for him to do so. He describes his treatment by his wife's relatives at Shaw Bridge on his return, and admits that strong language was used On both sides, for which on his side, he has repeatedly expressed his regret. He denies the brutality which Mrs. Jackson charges him with having been guilty of during the siege, and in proof of the disinterestedness of his action he says that while at Westview Mrs. Jackson offered him £3OO a year,which he refusSil, telling her that if he accepted such an offer it would at once be said he wanted her money and not herself. In conclusion, he says that he has always loved his wife and still loves her, and is ready, even now, to make up the unhappy quarrel. A sensation was caused it the Prince's Theatre, Black- burn, on Monday, by the service of a legal document from a local firm of solicitors formally prohibiting the singing of a songtextensively advertised, entitled "Mrs. Jackson." dealing with the Clitheroe abduction proceed- ings. Notwithstanding the prohibition the song was 4 given, the refrain
Woman is the master now,
Men must all obey. being taken up and sung uproariously by the densely packed audience.
