Radicals" that they are disposed to rub their eyes and ask if they have been dreaming when they find that a Tory Government is about to do what they have so often said ought never to be done. They are pretty well used to "jumping Jim Crow " ; but they cannot as yet reconcile themselves to this particular jump. What becomes now of the stock sneer which is embodied in the remark that "if the working classes have education free,they will be wanting clothes free and food free ?" It is hard to be wounded with an arrow from their own quiver; but there is no help for it—unless they are honest enough to revolt against what they believe to be wrong. But they will not do that; they will grumble, and threaten, and some of them may go the length of forming a small cave; but if they do this they will come out of it at the eleventh hour, and vote Tory as they have always done. They will thus repeat themselves, as their leaders are repeating them- selves by stealing one of the principal planks from the Liberal platform as the time draws nigh for a General Election. It is not a reputable piece of business, but, leaving morals out of the matter, it is about the best thing the Tories can do. They know that as soon as they get their quietus at the polling booths, resistance is all over with them, and Free Education will be given by a Liberal Government, let them howl against it as they may. "Why not," they say, "anticipate the inevitable, and take credit for doing, ot trying to do, what must be a popular thing?" And so for the twenty-first time they have swallowed all their own formulas and decided to "shoot Niagara:' Just now curiosity is great as to the features of the Education Bill which is to be brought in after Whitsuntide. The Government know quite as well as the Opposi- tion that it is contrary to every sound principle of finance to make provision for popular expenditure without popular control ; and yet so little can the present Ministry be trusted to do the right thing that there is a growing suspicion that it is their intention to provide the money for Free Education without at the same time making provision for the election of representatives of the people on School Management Committees. But this wont do: "taxation withcut representation is tyranny." As we have for many years advocated Free Edu- cation in these columns, it is a pleasure to find that like the freeing of the Warrington Library, it will come with a rush at last ; and we venture to pre- dict that, after a short experience of the advantages of the reform, the mass of the people . will marvel that they should have so long tolerated the old System of school fees. Strictly speaking, there is no such thing as " free " education; it will still have to be paid for like free streets, free parks, free roads, and free bridges. The diffetence is that toll will be taken en masse instead of taking it person- ally in a costly, irritating, and mischievous way. If the right thing had been done at the right time, school fees would have been abolished from the moment education became compulsory. We have always contended and still contend, that it is, an injustice to the poor to insist that a small and perhaps broken income shall be still further re- duced, by school fees, when the money may be urgently wanted for the necessaries of life. It is not sufficient to say that Boards of Guardians are prepared to pay the fees in these cases. There are thousands of decent hard-working people who struggle on, and pinch and punish themselves, rather than make an application which is closely allied to pauperism. It thus happens that, when fees are not forthcoming, children are kept away from school. The child is punished &rough the poverty of the parent; and in the end the parent may be punished by being dragged before a bench of magistrates for not paying school fees when school fees ought not to have been paid. Added to this, there is the diminished school attendance; the friction between teachers and scholars; and the labour and loss of time of School Attendance Officers. We do not mean to say that we shall see nothing of this under Free Education, but we do say that these evils will be greatly les- sened. The odd thing is, that school fees, which havebeenthe bone of contention all along, actually amount to lessthan one-third of the cost of elemen- tary tuition. In one way and another—mainly by grants and School Board rates—the nation has been paying two-thirds of the total cost. This is a factor which people who object to Free Education never look fully in the face; they boggle over that other factor—the paltry one-third, which will, we trqst, ease the problem ere long by disappearing from it for ever. •

The Loss THERE is naturally a great deal of at discussion in Warrington as to Longford. the state of affairs at Longford and the fear is that the ratepayers do not even yet know the worst. What is known is certainly bad enough. According to the figures furnished last week by Councillor Stir% W GREEN who, as vice- ehairrnan of the Finance Committee, is in the pos- session of official information, the defieit on the year's working at Longford, as a manufactory of concentrated manure, was ascertained to be £Bl5 before the blunder in the stock was discovered. The amount of manure in stock, instead of being of the value of £2,265, was found to be £1,460 only, or a further deficit of £BO5, showing a total deficit of £1,620. To ascertain what is the full loss to the ratepayers—looking at Longford as a manu- factory which, they were told, was to be a profit to them—account must be taken of the sum of £l,OOO or more which has been paid in the shape of wages to the manager and men who have been engaged in the process of manufacture ; while at least £l,OOO more must be set down for interest and for depre- ciation of plant and buildings. As against this, the concern requires to be credited with the money received for the manure sold. It may be that the whole of the" 200 tons wrong" in stock-taking does not belong to the present year ; but if that be so it only partially affects the result. Viewed from any point of view, there is every need for a Committee of Inquiry. We understand that the Sanitary Com- mittee are disposed to furnish the Council, on Tues- day-next, with all the information they can give. This is the least they can do. What the ratepayers wish to know is not whether Longford can be made profitable that is out of the question—but whether, in the first place, it has become q, neces- sity of the situation, and, if so, whether the loss cannot be reduced by less bungling and better management.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

Another death in New York through a shock from an electric wire. Electricity is like fire in that it is a good servant but a bad master. It is a satisfaction to know that, with our slow and sure methods, we order these things better in Eng- land.

We are requested to state that the late Mr. Nay- lor's work on Tanning which was recently reviewed in our columns was printed by Messrs. Waterlow Bros. and Layton, and that it is-published by the " Leather Trades Circular and Review" of 57 Weston-st., Bermondsey.

Our Correspondent " Ruabon," writing in respect to the confirmation service at Stockton Heath, accepts the statement of Mr. Robert Davies that the Bishop was refreshed with tea and not with champagne. As to the cost of the Bishop's visit, he explains that, as his lordship receives a salary of £4,200 a year, £l2 is the cost of a day's service.

The doctrine that "the King can do no wrong" can be illustrated even in these days. Colonel Mitchell has found to his cost that he cannot compel the Secretary for War to reconsider his pension which, he thinks has been based on a wrong scale. The ruling of Divisional Court is that the Secre- tary for War is responsible in the matter to the Crown, and the Crown only. And the Crown of course can do no wrong.

The Emperor William and Prince Bismarck are radically different in many things, but they agree in paying the highest possible tribute to the character of the late Count Von Molke. The brilliant success of the great strategist excited the utmost admiration; but now that he has passed away it is pleasanter to think of him as the man who set an example to his kind by his sincerity and simplicity, and moderation in all things.

The members of the Miners' Association in the GoThorne district, have been provided with a check, to wear on their caps or jackets, to show that they belong to the association. Motley is not therefore the only wear ; and cabmen and 'busmen are to have somebody to keep them in countenance. It will be interesting to note how long this dis- tinctive feature is preserved. Like the wearing of the blue ribbon, these things have a tendency to die out. "They have their day and cease to be."

The evidence which Mr. Harford has given before the House of Commons Committee confirms all that has been previously heard as to the long hours of railway servants. He Mentioned the case of a signalman who had been on duty over 27 hours! What if there had been accident under the cir- cumstances? Would the man havebeen to blame, or the master? And, going deeper into the ques- tion, will Parliament not be to blame if matters are so left that it will be possible for such a thing to happen again?

Mr. Harford, who has been general secretary of the Railway Men's Union, is to be the Liberal candidate for Blackburn. He will have a hard fight of it; but the cotton operatives are well organized, and if they bend their backs to the job they can manage it. It is high time that railway servants had at least one spokesman in the House of Commons ; for the railway interest in the present Parliament has no fewer than 62 representatives,as against 57 in the House of 1885. In 1886, in this as in other matters, the country went one step backward.

The hobbledeboy-s of Stockton Heath are assert- ing themselves; they make life not worth living to some of the inhabitants; and it would seem from the reference to the matter at Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, that the police are unable to curb them as they can in towns. Still they can make the gang "move on " ; and if they are kept moving on they will be less capable of mischief. But the law must be extended, if it is not at pre- sent equal to grappling with these country corner- boys. k

• Ex-King Milan is like minor mortals in having troubles now and again about money matters. The other day he sought to cash a cheque, at Vienna, for 600,000 francs; but received one half only, the other being impounded to satisfy debts previously incurred by Ms Majesty. The ex-King's contention is that the debts in question should be paid by the Servian Government; but the bankers have their own view of the matter, and regard the bird in the hand as worth two in the bush. Perhaps the inci- dent will teach his Majesty to study economy; there is need for it.

The Archdeacon of Warrington, speaking at St. Helens on Thursday, in reference to Free Educa- tion said he should "like to:see an educational fran- chise, and thereby make the path of ignorance not so pleasant and profitable." This is the good old Tory doctrine of a hundred years ago: Presumptuous Poverty's quite appalling, Knock him over, and kick him for falling. But we got beyond that when household suffrage was adopted; and, since Ignorance as well as Knowledge was given a vote, there has been more education than was ever before known. The Arch- deacon must try again; the facts are against him this time.

Mrs. Jackson has certainly scored by her " Vin- dication ; and if her husband-in-law cannot make a better show in his "Reply" than by saying his application to his wife for money was "in the nature of a joke" he had better leave it alone. There seems, on both sides, to have been talk about Love with an eye all the time to the Lucre. The feeling against Mrs. Jackson amongst the masses is based on the conviction that she is not keeping her vow to take her husband for better or for worse. It is felt that it is not quite fair that a woman who happens to be "well off" should be able to be a law unto herself, whilst others in a similar plight have to "grin and 'bide."

The destruction by fire of High Legh church on Saturday, recalls the fact that the late Dr. Moffat, the celebrated Missionary, resided for a tinie at High Leigh when quite a young man. He was born in Scotland in 1795, and left his native land at the age of 1S to become under-gardener to Mr. Leigh. He lived in a lodge on the grounds, and it is stated that "the young gardener attracted the kindly notice of Mrs. Leigh, who lent him books, and encouraged him in his studious pursuits." He did not, however, retain the goodwill of his em- ployers, for he committed what in their eyes was a deadly sin—he became a Methodist!

Reading the life of the future great missionary, it is interesting to find that it was whilst at War- rington for the purpose of making a purchase that he received his missionary impulse. This was given through a missionary placard, in Bridge-st., of a meeting that was past. lie seems to have been spell-bound by it; but he adds :—" I hastened to obtain the trifle I wanted in the town, and re- turned to the placard and read it over once more, and now wended my solitary way homeward another man, or rather another heart." Warrington has a good deal to answer for, but it is something of a set-off that Moffat's call dates from his casual visit to the town.

Now that the facts as to the disaster at Mani- pur are known, it is seen that Mr. Quinton, the Chief Commissioner, was rash in his action to the verge of madness. He sacrificed his own life and the lives of others by attempting the impossible. It was preposterous to think of 450 British troops , overawing twice as many thousands of native soldiers, and yet this was the basis of Mr. Quinton's policy. Mrs. Grimwood, the wife of the Resident, behaved like a heroine • and a letter from Mr. Cal- vert, surgeon, shows that he, too, was in the thick of it; but he treats bullets as lightly as if they were pills. The material was splendid, but not even heroes can fight against such fearful odds as twenty to one.

The foreigner who leaves home to better his condition in a new and strange land is likely to have" the way out" for him made a little harder. A Committee of the United States Senate is at present engaged in considering how the door can best be closed in the face of immigrants who are wanting what is called" self-maintaining capacity." At home, Mr. Howorth,llll.P.,is directing attention to the influx into this country of destitute aliens. He proposes to bar their way in some degree by raising the naturalization fee from £1 to £lO. This would be hard on the stranger within our gates; but charity should begin at home. Besides, as Tennyson has it— That man's the best Cosmopolite Who loves his country best.

div.head: MAD KING OF BAVARIA
div.p: THE MAD KING OF BAVARIA

BERLIN, THURSDAY.—It is announced that King Otto of Bavaria, who has been insane and under restraint for many years, is now suffering from cedema of thd brain, and his condition is said to be much worse than the official and inspired newspapers admit.

div.head: POOR RATE FOR NORTON.
div.p: POOR RATE FOR NORTON.

The Runcorn magistrates, on Monday, sanctioned the levying of a poor rate of is. in the £ for the township of Norton. The assistant overseer said the rate last half- year was only 10d. and had the overseers not had a balance in hand, the rate would have been is. 2d. in the £.
SUCCESS OF A RUNCORN MUSIC STUDENT.

Among the names of those who succeeded in passing the recent senior examination of the Royal Academy and Royal College of Music, occurs that of Miss Augusta H. Jones, of 9, Stanley-villas, Runcorn, and we compliment her upon her achievement. Miss Isherwood was the teacher.

div.head: MAY DAY AT WIDNES,
div.p: MAY DAY AT WIDNES,

The "merrie'month of May" opened very inauspiciously. From an early hour,rain, until afternoon, descended in a drenching drizzle, and the display made by the carters and others incharge of horse flesh was seen unciar very unfavourable circumstances. Numerous animals were gaily decorated.
ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.

About four o'clock on Monday afternoon, John Heath, a shunter employed at the works of Messrs. Hall Bros. and Shaw, was 'found near the railway metals of the works, with one of his legs almost severed from his body, and he said he had been run over by a wagon. He was conveyed to the Accident Hospital, where he is under the tare of Dr. Hutchinson. It is feared that the limb will have to be amputated. The inan's home is at 60, Dick- son-st.
CHILD DROWNED AT FARNWORTH.

Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, on Tuesday, held an inquest at Farnworth on the body of Mary Ellen Jack- son, 16 months old, daughter of William Jackson, of 20 Upton Rocks. The deceased was playing with some other children in the garden, and after a time one of the children told the father his daughter was in the ashpit amongst the water. He found her lying face downwards in a pool of water 18 inches deep, and quite dead. It is believed deceased fell in whilst playing.—A verdict of accidental death was recorded. -
SPRING FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.
POSTPONEMENT OF LOCAL GOVERNMENT INQUIRIES.

Colonel Ducat, R.E., one of the inspectors of the Local Government Board, had arranged to hold an inquiry at Widnes Town Hall on Tuesday morning, into an applica- tion of the Local Board for sanction to borrow £9783 for works of street improvement, &c. Arrangements had also been made for holding an inquiry at Runcorn in the afternoon with regard to the application of the Commis- sioners for permission to borrow £245 for the purchase ef scavenging plaint. On Monday afternoon the Local Government Board telegraphed that owing to the illness of Colonel Ducat the inquiries must be deferred.

div.head: ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN VETERINARY SURGEON.
div.p: ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN VETERINARY SURGEON.

Mr. Fred. Yarwood, veterinary surgeon and cab pro- prietor, Albert-st., met with a very serious accident on Wednesday. He was driving with a pair of long reins a young unbroken colt, belonging to Mr. Jonathan Horsfield, and when he was just turning from Greenway road into Norman-road, a railway train passed under the Bridge, causing the horse to take fright. Mr. Yarwood maintained his hold of the reins, but the horse over- powered him, pulling him to the ground, and in its flight turned him round and round for a great number of times. The horse was secured, and Mr. Yarwood was taken home, where he now lies suffering from sprains and bruises on almost every part of his body, and many weeks will elapse before he will be able to leave his bed and resume his work. SPRING FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The annual meeting was held yesterday afternoon,when Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., was unanimously re-elected chairman. Mr. Oppenheim (the clerk pro tem.) pre- sented the statement of accounts for the past year. The receipts were as follows :—Received from rates £404 Os., fines £2l 9s. 91-d., catalogues £1 18s. 4d., old papers £4 14s. 4d., damages £1 3s. lid:, subscriptions £3 3s. 2d., total £445 10s. Bd. The expenditure amounted to the same total made up as follows :—Furniture and fittings £ll 16s. 5d., gas, water, and rates £3O 13s. 4d., books £l3B us. Bd., salaries £l2B 18s. 4d., insurance £1 65., printing and stationery £6 Bs. 11d., cleaning expenses £l5 125., magazines £6 Bs. id., newspapers £3B 14s. Bd., repairs and sundry expenses £5 2s. 2d., repayment of principal and interest £57 165., balance in hand £3 19s. The statement was adopted. A sub-committee was ap- pointed to make a selection of new books for purchas,.
WIDNES DIVISION CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION.

The annual meeting was held on Thursday night, in Widnes Conservative Club, under the presidency of Mr. Macgenzie Smith. Mr. Woodnorth, the secretary, read the annual report,which stated that the party had gained considerably in strength during the past year. Regret was expressed at the retirement of Mr. W. J. Stewart from the position of chairman of the Association.—On the proposition of Mr. Mather, Major Cross was unani- mously elected Chairman of the Association. Major Walker was appointed treasurer.—Mr. Lewis moved a resolution thanking Lord Salisbury for having acted as Pre3ident of the Association during the past year, and asking him to retain the position ; and also expressing confidence in Her Majesty's Government.—Mr. M. H. Larmore seconded the motion, which was adopted unani- mously.—Vice-presidents were elected as follows :—Sir A. B. Walker, Messrs. J. W. Moss, A. Fletcher, E. Banner, J. Pilkington, and J. R. Robertson. EMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia; San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Onion, American, and other lines.— John Walker, agent. "Examiner Office, Bewsov-st.. Warrington.—Advt. PHOTOGRAPHIC LECTURE AT RUNCORN. Last evening week Mr. Charles.A. Timmins gave a lec- ture and lime-light exhibition of views of the Manches- ter Ship Canal in those schools. The slides 114 in num- ber, were those exhibited quite recently by Mr. Timmins at the Photographic Exhibition, held in the Walker Art Gallery at Liverpool, and doubtless the very flattering criticism passed upon them by the Liverpool Press, combined with his popularity in Runcorn, and his knowledge of the canal works, secured for him the large and appreciative audience that was present. The chair was occupied by Mr. John Meadowcroft, who in a few well-selected sentences introduced the lecturer to his audience' and incidentally remarked upon the success that had been achieved by Mr. Timmins at Liverpool by his perseverance in the photographic art. The brilliancy and clearness of the slides, many of them being of familiar spots,were greatly appreciated and acimired,and a number of them woe deservedly applauded. When- ever an opportunity for the explanation of any point of interest occurred, Mr. Timmins availed himself of it. At the close a vote of thanks was carried by acclamation to Mr. Timmins for his lecture, to the Chairman for pre- siding, and to each and every other lady id gentleman who had taken any part in making the entertainment a success.

A RUNCORN FLATMAN HEAVILY FINED. Before Mr. Gossage and Mr. Deacon at Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, James Wardle, a flatman, of Run- corn was charged with having, on the 24th March, when in charge of the Annie Maria, refused to obey the orders of the lock master of Widnes Docks, and for having obstructed the entrance of a vessel into a lock at Widnes preparatory to its entering the river from the Widnes and St. Helens Canal. Mr. Preston, jun., prosecuted on be- half of the London and North-Western Railway Company, who own the canal and docks,and stated that on the date mentioned the Annie Maria and another flat named the Milly were lying in the canal. Milly was loaded,but the Annie Maria was not. For 20 years it had been an estab- lished custom that loaded flats should tako precedence of light flats in going in or out of the locks, so as to have advantage of deep water; but the defendant refused to make room for the Milly, and in consequence that boat lost a tide.—Mr. Birkett, Liverpool, for the defence said the defendant had acted under a misapprehension.—Mr. Gossage said it was a very serious matter to cause a vessel to lose a tide, for if her captain did not arrive at Liverpool at a certain time he might lose the shipping of his boat's cargo,and there might not be another ship for a year. It was not stated to have been so in this case, hut such a result was possible.--The defendant was fined £5 and costs, and the money was paid. SPRING FASHIONS now Showing at J. lc. W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Aivt.

FOOTBALL AND THE RUNCORN NURSE FUND. With the object of increasing the Runcorn District Nurse Fund, the Committee of the Runco.rn Football Club arranged a match between the local 15 and a team made up of players from Widnes and Warrington, which took place on Wednesday evening. Although rain descended throughout the whole of the play, there was a good at- tendance of spectators, aid it is estimated that the re- ceipts will amount to £5O. Miss Jo net Taylor, daughter of Mr. S. Thylor,chairman of the Board of Commissioners, lent grace and interest to the occasion by starting the match. An interesting and well contested game resulted ia favour of the home team, 1 goal 1 try 3 minors, to Widnes and Warrington 3 trios 3 minors. Neither side had its. full compliment of men. The final score was :—St. Mary's 2 gdals, 1 try, 2 minors, Widnes 1 try, minor. SPRING FASHIOSS now Showing at J. Fc. W. div.head: PRESENTATION TO A PRESSUAN.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO A PRESSUAN.

On Thursday, Mr. J. H. Ridgway, reporter, was pre- sented with a fountain pen holder, with iridium-pointed gold pen, and a purse of gold, as a token of esteem and in acknowledgement of his four years' service on the Runcorn Press, on the occasion of his leaving the town to undertake the management of the "Harborne Herald," a branch paper of the Birmingham Times Company. The subscribers were numerous, and included the names of members of the Improvement Commissioners and Board of Guardians. There was no formal presentation, but a number of friends assembled at the railway station to bid him good bye and wish him success in his new sphere. BASSINF.TTES.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt. THE ELECTORAL Di-VISIONS OF THE LANCASHIRE

• COUNTY COUNCIL. The Parliamentary Committee of the Lancashire County Council state that they are glad to report that the Local Government Board have issued an order increasing the representation on the County Council from 102 to 105, and re-dividing the elec- toral divisions in accordance with the resolution of the Council held on the 7th of February last. The order will take effect on and from the Ist of Novem- ber next.
LAWN MOWERS.—Garland, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington, and at Barlestown.—Advt..
BICYCLE RACE.

A race took place' on the Prescot-road, on Thurs- day afternoon, between John Thomas Fletcher, cab proprietor, and Ernest Turley, a slender-built young man, both of St. Helens. Fletcher was given half a mile start, the winning point being the King's Arms, Prescot. About halt a mile from the finish Fletcher fainted, and Turley was declared the winner. The race was for teas. Fletcher rode a tricycle and Turley a safety bicycle.

FATAL SWINGBOAT ACCIDENT AT LEIGH. A shocking accident, which terminated fatally shortly afterwards, happened to a lad named Thomas Yates, at Leigh, a little after eigpt o'clock on Saturday evening. The lad was standing on the fairground, and was struck on the head by a swing- boat. Five men at once conveyed him to the sur- gery of Dr. Hall, who, upon examination, found that his brains were hanging out of the wound, and that the case was hopeless. The unfortunate youth, aged leven years, was an orphan, and lived with his brother-in-law, at Chapel-st. This is the second fatality from the same source in eight days, a girl having been killed at the Tyldesley fair on tLe 18th inst.
SPRING FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. DurToN'S, Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Adv. FINANCIAL REFORM ASSOCIATION.

Mr. E.K. Muspratt, presiding on Wednesday night over the annual .meeting of the Financial Reform Association in the Rotunda Hall, Liverpool,declared that the policy of the present Government was en- tirely a landlord policy. After speaking of the pro- posed Van and Wheel Tax and the proposed com- pensation to publicans, Mr. Musprati, expressed his conviction that if the Liberal party would under- take to oppose these financial proposals of the Government on every occasion they would of neces- sity find a large support from the Tory party. SUICIDE AT PARR. James Harrison, a day wagernan in a colliery, of 128, Broad Oak-road, Parr, committed suicide on Wednesday. Deceased, who was 35 years of age, was internally injured while following his occupa- tion about twelve months ago, and has since been out of work. He visited his mother's house, a few doors from his home, on. Wednesday forenoon, and itfter some conversation left, stating that he wait re- turning to his wife. Five minutes later, however, his mother saw him hanging by a handkerchief tied round his neck and fastened to a hook in an entry leading to the back of the premises. An alarm was at once made, and deceased was cut down by a man named Woodward, but he died immediately after- wards.

AN OUTCOME OF THE GARSTON STRIKE. An important decision as regards the shipping trade was given by Mr. Justice Lawrance in the Queen's Bench Division on Saturday. The case was that of Jones v. London and North-Western Rail- way which was recently tried before his lordship at Liverpool. During the recent strike of labourers at Garston Dock the plaintiffs' vessels Ricardo and Bergamo were considerably delayed in discharging, and demurrage was claimed. It was alleged on be- half of the plaintiffs that the scarcity of efficient men was the fault of the defendant company, who had locked their men out, and also refused to let the plaintiffs employ their own men. Mr. Justice Lawrence awarded plaintiffs £125, accompanied by a declaration of rights and an injunction, the terms of which will be settled hereafter. THE NEW ST. lIELENS RAILWAY.

Mr. Henry Seton Karr, M.P., chairman of the directors of the Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancashire Railway, accompanied by Councillor Joseph Beecham, Mr. 11. S. Oppenheim, solicitor, and Mr. Amos Hanson, surveyor, proceeded to Hay- dock, on Monday, to inspect the work in progress. The line will run on the north side of Parr, crossing to the south side of the main road at Redgate Bridge, where it again crosses to the north of the main road. At this point the Haydock Station NI ill be erected. Continuing to the north of Hay- dock Lodge Asylum, the line will pass through Ash- ton and on to Golborne, joining that portion which has already been constructed, and form a junction With the Wigan Junction Railway. The work will now be pushed forward rapidly.: A BURTONWOOD BOY THREATENS SUICIDE. It will be will be within the recollection of our readers that some months ago two girls who lived at Burtonwood, committed suicide in a very deli-.i berate manner,by drowning themselves in the canal. One of the girls was named Andrews, the daughter , of a collier of that name, living in Tan House-lane, ' Burtonwood. It has now transpired that last week another of the children left the house with a simi- lar intention, but was luckily prevented just in time. It appears that Henry Andrews, 11 years of age, the deceased girl's brother, one day last Week was absent from school without his father's per- mission. For this he was chastised by his father, , and still smarting under the indignity, he said he would not be thrashed again by his father, as lie would go and drown himself. He then rushed oht of the house, and made off as fast as he could, towards Cooper's pit, which is the same pool of water that his sister made her first attempt in. Another younger sister told a neighbour what her brother had said, and this person called to a lad named Cooper to follow the intending suicide. Cooper made off and came up with Andrews, just before he reached the pit, and with difficulty dragged him back to his home. Ile was then sent to school, but his sister had to go and see that he came home safely. The lad persisted in saying that he would make away with himself yet. DEATH OF A CHESHIRE POLICE CONSTABLE. The death took place on Monday last at Hoole, near Chester, of John Broady, a police constable in the Cheshire Constabulary. The deceased, who was 24 years of age, was taken ill some fcur weeks ago, and was attended during his illness by Dr. Archer. Up to the morning of his death he seemed to have considerably imuoved, and hopes were entertained of his ultimate recovery, but later on the symptoms grew worse, and he quietly and peacefully passed away at 5 o'clock in the afternoon. He leaves a widow and one child. The deceased officer joined the force in 4111 y, 1887, and was quickly transfered to Egremont, from which place, on account of his untiring zeal and thrift, he was again transferred in March, 1889, to Chester as an assistant clerk in the Chief Constable's office,a post he has creditably filled, from that time tit) to his death. By his ivillingneas and obedience he soon won the esteem and confid- ence of his superior officers, and his loss is deeply deplored. His body was removed to Lymn, his native place, on Thursda3 morning and interred in the Lymn Churchyard. A large number of his fellow constables, as well as friends and relatives, were present. The service, which was choral, was con- ducted by the curate,and the choir of which he was formerly a member, sang a hymn at the graveside. A large number of costly wreaths and crosses were sent by the relatives and friends of the deceased, prominent amongst them being one from Chester, specially made by the noted Messrs. Dickson's, Nurserymen, which bore the following inscription. "From comrades at Chester, as a last mark of respect and esteem." 23rd April, 1891.

BY IN OCCASIONAL CORIINSPONDiNT.

The correspondence which has taken place in this journal on the subjeet of Sunday trains, shows that there is a widespread feeling in favour of breaking down the present system of isolation. Summer is. approaching—all too slowly indeed, but still ap- proaching—and the denizens of dingy Runcorn will long to be away from the murky. atmesphere in which they earn their daily bread, and to breathe the purer air amid the more joyous and beautiful scenery of the surrounding country. Will some sympathising member of the Board oi Coninais- sioners bring the matter forward at the meeting on Thursday, and induce the members to make an en.: deavour to obtain for Runcorn the privilege of a fe ' trains from Liverpool to Chester, and vice versa on Sundays. It is most unfair-that towns much smaller and less important than Runcorn should have con- veniences that Runcorn is a total stranger to; and a proper representation to the present chairman of the Railway Company, would, I am confident, result in the concession asked for being granted. Even the " dodger" from Ditton to Ilelsby would be lit better than the present total want of railway com- munication on the one day on which the working- classes have the most time and liberty to visit their distant friends or to worship at nature's shrine. Of Mr. John Simpson's theological opinion no one in Runcorn can for a moment be in doubt. As in other things of this life, Mr. Simpson is thorough in his religion, and by his actions he shows himself a firm believer in the creed, polity, and policy of the Wesleyan Methodists. his definite pronouncement at the Frodsham Bazaar on Wednesday will cause no surprise, nor will the fact that he views with in- dignation andsontempt the exerticns made by some sects to entice children from the Sunday Schools which they attend, and the attempts made to in- duce their elders to forsake the faith they espouse by means which Mr. Simpson and the Wesleyan body generally would scorn to use. He declared such attempts to be contrary to the spirit of Chris- tianity, and very justly said that without wasting energy in prosleytising them, there was ample scope for all denominations in the work of rescuing the sinner. _

Although Mr. Simpson spoke in general terms, there is no doubt that his remarks were intended to have a particular application to the locality, and perhaps those concerned will carefully consider the matter and act accordingly. If followers of the Founder of Christianity Cannot live in amity and love, and work hand in hand for the universal I brotherhood of man, where must we look? I Under present circumstances, when a reforming I spirit appears to be very much abroad amongst judges and magistrates on the subject of the licensing laws, holders of licenses cannot be too careful. A fortnight age Inspector Bowyer found two drunken men in Rutter's vaults, and on the I table before them were a quart jug and glass,lwhich was the common drinking vessel for the company, a custom, which; although it may seem jovial and friendly,is not likely to be adopted by polite society. In face of the declaration of one of the persons who had drunk not wisely but too well, that he had paid for that quart, the landlady sought to prove that a sober man in the room had found the neces- sary coppers, and that the other men were turned thirsting away. The Bench's knowledge of human nature, and their sifting of the evidence, led them to a different conclusion, and Mrs. Priss had to con- tribute upwards of £2 IA the county funds, and accept an intimation from the Bench that she was lucky to escape so lightly. An endeavour is being made to endow the Run- corn District Nurse Fund, and several hundred pounds have been raised with that end in view. Last year Runcorn Football Club, by means of a match, contributed about 1:45, and a game was played on Wednesday last for the same purpose, but it is not likely that after expenses are paid se large a sum will be turned over on the present occasion. Much dissatisfaction has been expressed at the raising of the price of admission to double that ordinarily demanded. Many working-men were thereby prevented from attending, the charge being beyond their means, and others stayed away as a protest against such a course. Were it not for the support of the working population, football would speedily die, and it was very ill-judged policy to debar so many from aiding a worthy object and en- joying an hour's recreation. Who was responsible for the innovation?

It would seem to be a dangerous custom to leave a horse and conveyance in front of the Widnes Con- servative Club. On Thursday night Mr. Griffiths of The Manor, Hale, attended the annual meeting of the Conservative Association, and afterwards spent a fleeting hour at a smoking concert. At eleven o'clock his horse and gig were brought to the en- trance of the Club, and an obliging individual—evi- dently a designing:Radical—proffered to hold the noble animal's head. Confidence was placed in his honesty, but when Mr. Griffiths came forth some minutes afterwards, horse, gig, and custodian were non-eBl and a search did not reveal their whereabouts. Information was given to the police, and Mr. Grif- fiths completed his homeward journey in a hired cab. Superintendent Noblett set his emissaries to. work, and yesterday the thief was caught at Bootle, and the horse and gig, which is valued at £5O re- covered uninjured. Mr. Griffiths will perhaps. ex- ercise more care next time he spends a convivial evening at his Club, and place his trust in an indi- vidual who has some regard for the sacred rights of property.

div.head: RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA CLA.SSES.
div.p: RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA CLA.SSES.

These classes which have enjoyed an enviable reputation for some years past, have just brought to a close one of the most successful sessions ever held. During the winter 22, entered for the junior examination and 19 passed, 25 entered for the ele- mentary and 24 passed ; 3 entered and three passed in elementarytheory ; 5 i entered and 5 passed n the first grade staff notation; 6 entered for the inter- mediate and 5 passed, and 3 entered and 3 passed in intermediate theory. .Mr. John Holford G.T.S.C., the teacher, is to be congratulated on the success of his exertions. With the intention of providing a pleasant evening's amusement, and of presenting the certificates to the students, a concert was held on Monday evening, in Runcorn Publio Ball, and a large audience assembled. The charming cantata " Sherwood's Queen had been chosen for representation, and the joint work of Mr. T. M. Pattison and Mr. A. J. Foxwell, was executed with a vigour and harmony that was highly creditable to the choir of upwards of 100 pupils, and gave much pleasure to the auditory. The principal parts in the cantata were ably taken by Miss Heatherington

(Maid Marion); Miss Ainsworth (the widow); Mrs. Leathwood (Alice) ; Mr. E. Worrall (Robin Hood) ; Mr. J. Leathwood (Allan-a-dale) ; Mr. James Weedall (Will Scarlet) ; Mr. Walter Dutton (Little John) ; Mr. A. Shing- ler (Friar Tuck) ; and Messrs. Evans, Morton,and Dutton (widow's sons). The whole performance was bright and tuneful, and well deserved encores were frequently acccrded. The second part of the programme was of a miscellaneous chhracter. During an interval, Mr. Hol- ford, the teacher and conductor, invited Dr. McDougall to come forward and distribute the certificates to the students. NI% Holford explained that the certit. cates were a distinguishing characteristic of tbr..i Tonic sol-fa method, and enabled the progredsl of the pupil t 9 b gauged in the varioui stages by the eiatnination3 in the theory and practice of music. --Dr. McDougall then distributed the prizes, and in a subsequent speech bore testimony to the . wide appreciation of the talented and successful ' manner in which Mr. liolforcl had conducted these classes and developed year by year this important branch of education. Nine yeari a,go, when Mr. tfolford 'started, theclass numbered only 41 ; ithad now attained '!to 121. (Applause.) He thought they would admit that more encouragement should be given 0 Mr. Hol- ford and as he was doing a great public service; lie thought the Government should recognise it in some substantial manner. They should use their influence to induce a paternal Government to lend its support to this movement and not leave the whole burden on the shoulders of Mr. Holford. (Applause.) In acknow- ledging the compliment paid him. Mr. Holford remarked that this;vvas the jubilee year of tbe tonic sol-fa, and he hoped in the autumn with the assistance of his classes to celebrate the occasion in a fitting manner. He hoped they would all help to make the demonstration a success. (Applause.)

div.head: WESLEYAN CENTENARY BAZA_.X.R AT
div.p: WESLEYAN CENTENARY BAZA_.X.R AT
FRODSHANI.

A two days' bazaar was opened on Wednesday afternoon, in the Wesleyan School, Chapel-lane, Frodsham. The promoters had a two-fold object— firstly to celebrate the centenary of the death of the venerable founder of the Wesleyan Society—the Rev. John A esley, MA., and also the centenary of ' the establishment ot Methodism in Frodsham. Of course the end and aim of all bazaars is the raising of money, and this was no exception to the rule. Trinity Chapel, a handsome structure in stone, the gift of the late Mr. Thomas If azlehurst, in the year 1872, requires certain structural repairs and also a thorough renovation, while the old chapel in Chapel- lane, which is now used for the numerous purposes of a sehoo‘and also the Trust property required repair. For carrying out this necessary and important work £4OO is needed, and it is hoped that the bazaar will be the means of raising a good sum towards that amount. The ladies connected with the chapel and school had or some time past been assiduously at work preparing for the event, and the result as displayed in the schoolroom, was a great compliment tQ ttrir labOtM, A large , Company assembled to witness the opening ceremony, ' friends being present from Runcorn. 'The Rev. H. Burson (Runcorn) offered up prayer, and then the Rev. P. Pizey, the minister, introduced Mr. John Simpson, of Dunsdale, to open the bazaar.—Mr. Simpson, after ex- pressing.his cordial approval of and sympathy with the object of the bazaar,said it was the duty of the trustees, out of respect to the memory of Mr. Thomas Hazlehurst (applause) who so kindly presented the chapel, to take care that the building was kept in a state of proper repair, land that it should never be less beautiful than it was at the time he presented it to the circuit. (Applause.) It was very desirable that every means should be used to promote the interests of the cause which he believed they all as Methodists had so much at heart, and he thought they ought to make their chapels and schools as pleasant and attractive as they possibly could. (Hear, hear.) It was quite natural that one should think most highly of that branch of the church with which one was identified and he thought in Wesleyan Methodism they had a system which was superior to any other church organisation. They had safeguards against the teaching of error; they had a system of discipline both for ministers and laymen wilich were in his opinion superior to what they saw in other churches. If they went into a 'Methodist Chapel they did not feel any doubt as to what doctrines they would hear. 1 hat could not be said of all places of worship. They had an arrangement for employing the various talents which existed amongst them, for promot- ing the best interests of those with whom they were associated, and for seeking and saving those who were lost. He had been a member of the Wesleyan Methodist ! Church between 50 and 60 years. (Applause.) He had known a gpod deal of some other churches,and that was his deliberate opinion. But though he thought so highly of Methodism, he had not the slightest wish to attract children from other schools to attend theirs—(hear, hear) —or members of other congregations to attend their ser- vices. He was sometimes told that there were places when such a course was systematically carried on—cer- tainly not by Methodists—and great efforts and all sorts of means used to rob other churches. He considered it a mean and contemptible thing to do. (Hear, hear.) He should scorn to lift a finger to induce one single child to come from any other Sunday School to a Wesleyan ' School, or to try to draw away one single member of any congregation to attend any of their Methodist services. He did not care what church it was or who the persons were who acted thus, he considered it contrary to the spirit of Christianity. (Hear, hear.) There was ample scope for them all to do all they possibly could without interfering with each other. (flear,hear.) In conclusion, Mr. Simpson expressed the hope that better days were in store for the Methodists of Frod- sham than had been seen hitherto, and that the bazaar would be a success. He was glad to hear there was to be no raffling in connection with that bazaar—(hear, hear)— there was to be nothing but legitimate selling and buy- ing, and buyingand selling. (Hear. hear.) Hedeclared the bazaar open amid applause.—Mr. Pizey announced that Mr. Simpson had contributed a Bank of England note of £2O to the bazaar.—Mr. S. Woodward (of Kings- ley) moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Simpson for opening the bazaar, remarking that they ought to be thankful to him for his genuine deslaration with regard to Methodist doctrine, Methodist polity, and Methodist policy. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. Richard Proud seconded the motion,which was carried unanimously, and Mr. Simpson having ac- knowledged the compliment, the ladies commeneed the ' sale of their wares. There were six stalls of the usual character; on which were displayed a charming variety of plain, fancy, and artistic needlework, and a multitude of other articles. There was also a refreshment stall well stocked with appetising edibles. The stallholders were Mrs. W. Andrews, Mrs. J. A. Bennett, Mrs. Bow- den, Mrs. Carter, Mrs. Collinson, Mrs. Conway, Mrs. Firbank, Mrs. Howard, Mrs. Jones, Mrs. Kent, Mrs. Pizey, Mrs. Proud, Mrs. Rimmer, Mrs. Robinson„ Mrs. Shore, Mrs. Wrench, Miss Andrews, Miss Challoner, Mrs. Jeynes, Mrs. Leycock, and Miss Sharrock. One of the great attractions of the bazaar was" The circuit Quilt," which had proved a most fruitful source of income. It was exhibite(bin a classroom amid was visited by hun- dreds in the course of the day. The front of the quilt is of French linens in art shades of terracotta, duck egg, pale fawn, and blue, and consisted of geometrical designs stitched on with amber silk and tinsel cord. In the border were three inscriptions and a capital repre- sentation of Trinity Chapel. The inscriptions were "Worked by Mrs. W. Robinson in aid of Trinity Trust Bazaar." Wesleyan Centenary Bazaar opened April 29, 1891, and: purchased by J. Shnosoa Esq., and presented to Trinity Wesleyan Circuit." All those persons who had subscribed to the bazaar were honoured by having their names recorded on the quilt, and Mrs. Robinson had succeeded in working in needle- work 512 names in plain but graceful characters. The amount raised by this means was £52. There was also a "Beehive," presided over by the following:—" Queen Bees" Miss Agnes Wrendti, Miss Emily Bewden, Miss Jenny Carter, Miss Lilly Edmonds, Miss Ruth Littler, Miss Eliza Sharrock, Miss Kitty Robinson, 'Ass Gertrude Worrall, Miss Maggie Isaac.—Other attractions were provided in the shape of vocal and instrumental music, shadowgraphy, a toy symphony,&c.
DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. E. A. WRIGHT OF FRODSHAM.

The mortal remains of Mr. Edward Abbott Wright, J.P., of Castle Park, Frodsham, were interred in their last resting place on Thursday afternoon, in Overton churchyard. Mr. Wright who had attained the patriarchal age of 82 years, died on Friday last after a long illness, and Fredsham has lost a man of great wealth and influence. He was a native of Oldham, in Lancashire, where he was born on the 7th November, 1808, and when only a few months old he had the misfortune to lose his father. After six years' widowhood, his mother married Mr. James Collinge, who subsequently became identified with the cotton trade as a spinner, and Mr. Wright was a witness of the scenes of violence cuised by the introduction of the power loom. tinder the impression that the introdu- tion of steam power was injurious to their interests, working-men stormed cotton mills and smashed machinery, and the mill with which Mr. Wright's stepfather was connected did not escape, but the calling out of the military and the read • log of the Riot Act soon quelled the disturbance. Some idea of the bitterness of .the contest may be ob- tained from the fact that one day while Mr. Wright was shaking hands with his schoolmaster at his stepfather's house:, a bullet catne crashing through the window, hap- pily withoutdoing any injury. It was not for ten years after these events that Mr. Wright, who had for some years acted as a manager, became a ixartner with his stepfather, the title of the firm being Messrs. Col/inge and Lancashire; and to him belongs the credit of having first attempted to draw up a list of wages which should he satisfactory to masters and men for spinning. In 1866 Mr. Wrht retired from business, and took up his permanent residenceat Castle Park, Frodsham.which he had purchased a few years previously. In Oldham he had taken an active part in public affairs,and had served his fellow - men as councillor, overseer, and magis- trate, and at the time of his death he was the father of the Oldham °Borough Beach. On taking up his residence at Frodsham, Mr. Wright was at once made a magistrate for the County of Chester,

and he zealously and faithfully fulfilled the duties of the post up to within a few months of his deatt. Man ex- qfficio member ot the Board of GuardiP.:„s, he took a most active part in the business of the °.ssess on en t Committee, and in parochial matters genie :ally he took a keen interest. He was a Churchman an!)., a Conservative, and for many years was the Chai7man of the Conservative Association. He wasalso senior executive councillor of the Frod- shrilfb'jitation of the Primrose League. In 1836 Mr. ~, Z4,lt was married to Mary, daughter of Mr. Henry rjerry. of Golden Square, London, who pre-deceased him by 23 years. Ells only son died at 15 years of age, bnt there are four daughters left to mourn his loss. The funeral took place on Thursday, and the following gentle- men met at the Park Gates and walked in procession iii front of the hearse :—Mr. James Reynolds, J.P., Mr. Charles Reynolds, J.P., Mr. A. Thomas, J.P.. Dr. Steele, J.P., Rev. Dr. Preston, Dr. Robinson, Colonel Ashton; Messrs. A. Linaker, H. G. Linaker, H. iley, G. Glsaves, S. Davies, T. D. Timmins, S. Walker, J. W. Bothwell, R. Bate, Drill-Sergeant Evans, S. Clarke, J. Rigby, junr.. J. , ritinler, J. Higginson, J. Delamere, H. Davies, G. Whit- low, J. Eyes, J. Johnson, J. Aston, J. Forster, J. Blease, W. Davies, J. Edwards, F. W. Dunsford, R. Holland, W. IH. Pickering, Sze. Fpllowing the hearse were seven carriages. The first carriage (Miss Wright's) contained: Miss Wright, Miss E. Wright, Mrs. Weaver, Dr. Weaver; 2nd carriage: Miss Weaver, Miss Annie Weaver, Mr. Collinge, Mr. Edward Weaver; 3rd carriage: Miss Harriet Weaver, Mr. George Garrett, Miss Maud Weaver, and Mr. F. K. Weaver ; 4th carriage: Mr. Alf. Weaver, Mr. Harold Weaver, Mr. Robinson, Mr. Ascroft, and the Rev. A. P. Reynolds (vicar of Kingsley) ' • sth carriage: Mr. Wrigley, Mr. Henry Wrigley, Mr. Knowles, and Mr. Bartley Dennis; 6th carriage: Mr. Clegg, Mr. Lees Knowles, Mr. C. E. Linaker, and Mr. Whitmore; 7th carriage (Mrs. Hayes) : Mrs. Thompson, Mrs. Black, and Miss Ann Stephenson. Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. John Simp- son had also sent their private carriages as a mark of respect. Before the mourners left the house the Rev. Mr. Reynolds conducted a short service in the dinning room, and he also assisted the Rev. H. B. Blagg in the obsequies in Overton Church and at the grave side. The coffin, which was of a most elaborate description, was covered with wreaths sent by relatives and friends, and it consisted of a shell enclosed with lead, brown oak panels, fumed oak styles, ebonised mouldings, brass mountings. Messrs. Robert Garnett and Sons, of War- rington, carried out the funeral arrangements.

div.head: ELECTION OF WHITLEY SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: ELECTION OF WHITLEY SCHOOL BOARD.

The triennial 'election of five members of the United District of Whitley School Board, which in- cludes the townships of Higher and Lower Whitley, took place on Friday last week. There were seven candidates in the field, and feeling ran high as to their respective merits. It was charged to the discredit of the members of the old Board that they had no young children, and canvassing was keenly and extensively in- dulged in by the whole of the candidates. The excite- ment of the contest VIRS added 0 4;7 the strained relations that exist between several of the gentlemen' concerned and by the fact that legal proceedings for slander were threatened. The presiding officer was Mr. A. Linaker (solicitor, Runcorn) who was assistedby Mr. H. Wright as poll clerk. Mr. J. Longland (of Warring- ton) was the personation agent for several candidates. The hours of polling were from 12 noon to 8 p.m., and immediately after the close of the poll Mr. H. G. Linaker, the returning officer, had the votes counted, and declared the result as f•llows to a large crowd of ratepayers : Mr. H. Nield J.P. Rev. J. J. Bryant W. Priestner
J. Barber 35. . There are 120 voters in the district, and 96 polled, and there were only four spoiled papers.
WIDNES PErtY SKSSIONS. THASDAY.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. H. Wade
Deacon.

DRUNKENNESS.—For the 57th time Edward Godfrey was summoned to the Court, and he was fined 7s. 6d. for being drunk and disorderly. A similar penalty was im- posed upon James Rogers for a like offence, and Henry Halsall was fined ss. and costs.

BREACH OF THE PEACE. —James Boyd, Walmsley-st., was charged with committing a breach of the peaco,and he was bound over to be of good behaviour for three mo,nths. FlRE.—Mary Hannen and David Jones were each fined, is. and costs for permitting the chimnies of their respec- tive dwellings to be on fire. DISMISSED.—Bridget Mannion summoned Mary Dunni- gan, of s,Railway-st., for using threats towards her, and the Bench, after hearing a number of witnesses,dismissed the case.

A GANG OF YOUNG THIEVES.—Seven boys, whose ages ranged from 12 to 15 years, named Patrick Hanerty, John Kelly, Patrick Hooligan, Thomas Nearny, Thomas Cain, John Welsh, and John A. Makin, were charged with stealing a quantity of old iron from the works of Messrs. Muspratt and Sons. The charge against Nearny was withdrawn,and he gave evidence as to the theft,and said the iron was sold to a man named Devine.—James Devine. Victoria-st., marine store dealer, admitted pur- chasing the iron, and said the boys told him they had picked it off the tips. He paid them is. 6d.—Superin- tendent Noblett said he was undecided whether Devine ought not to be in a different position. He had not acted creditably, and he should ask the Bench to disallow his expenses.—ln reply to the Bench, Devine said it was not his custom to buy such large pieces of iron from boys.— The defendants were ordered to come up foL judgment when called upon.—Andrew Fitzharris (12) as charged with stealing a piece of timber worth 6d. from Messrs. Muspratt's works. He was dealt with in a similar manner to the other boys. CIIARGE OF ASSAULT.—Robert Bradbury, Church-st., Farnworth, was summoned for assaulting a married woman named Elizabeth Beasley. It was alleged that when complainant went to empty her teapot at her yard gate, the defendant struck her, and knocked her to the ground.—Complainant said Bradbury claimed the land, and it was to assert her right that she went there.—Mr. Knowles for the defence submitted that as there was a question of title involved the Bench had no power to deal with the case.—The case was dismissed.

div.head: PENKETIL
div.p: PENKETIL
POOR RATE FOR PENKKTIL

On the application of Mr. T. H. Wilson, the assist- ant overseer, two county magistrates, Messrs. Ed. Greenall and John White, on Wednesday sanctioned the laying of a poor rate for the township of Penketh, for the current half-year, of is. in the X. It is estimated to produce £378 93. 6d. There were no arrears.

div.head: LITE MR. CHADWICK.
div.p: THE LITE MR. CHADWICK.

On Thesday the flag was flying at half-mast at the Conservative Club, Stocks-lane, Penketh, as a mark of respect to the late Mr. G. E. Chadwick, of Ferndale, Bold Heath, whose funeral took place at Farnworth. Mr. Chadwick had been unwell for some time, and his death, which took place at Blackpool on Saturday, is much regretted by the local Conservative party, as he took great interest in the work of the association. THE PENKETH PAROCH7AL COMMITTEE.

It is stated that the inhabitants of the township are expressing their regret that the Board of Guar- dians, or the Rural Sanitary Authority, at their last meeting,did not re-appoint the above Committee or appoint another. All the members of the Parochial Committee are sorry that the late Chairman- (Mr. J. C. Routledge) resigned the position he has gratuit- ously and ably filled, being untiring in his exer- tions during the carrying out of the drainage scheme, which has saved the township many hun- dreds of pounds. It is thought that the Parochial Committee ought not to have been dismissed, because they are under a prospective promise to provide a similar drainage scheme for the north por- tion of Penketh, contiguous to Sankey, along the brook that empties itself at Pool Mouth. This por- tion is without a drainage scheme, and being an improving part of the township—houses are in process of building now and others are contem- plated—the property and land owners will require provision to be made for them, as they contributed to the cost of the present scheme, which does not help them at all. Other matters respecting the care of the flushing tanks and the pipes require attention.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

FIRE AT 11)EL HALL, KINGSLEY.—Late on Saturday evening a fire broke out on the farm buildings in the occupation of Mr. E. G. Steward, from some unknown cause. Willing hands from the neighbourhood were soon at work attempting to quench the flames by the good supply of water which, fortunately, there is on the pre- mists. Ultimately this was accomplished, but not until great damage had beon sustained to portions of the build- ings, in one of which was stored some 600 bushels of wheat. The loss is fully covered by insurance.
