BEFORE THE M.A.GISTRATES.
DOG MUZZLING A FARCH IN 'WARRINGTON.

At the Borough Police Court, en Monday, Matthew Knowles 26, Allen-st., was charged with allowing. _his dog to be at large unmuzzled, in Sankey-st., on the 22nd inst.—Police-Sergeant Chandler deposed that seeing the dog in charge of a young lady, with its muzzle off. The muzzle would not stay on, but was round its neck. The young lady said the muzzle was the same as those used by other people and it would do.—Alderman Sutton said in his opinion the dog was just as effectively muzzled as i nine out of ten dogs in the town. Muzzling n Warring- ton was really a perfect farce,in his opinion. Dogs could bite just as well with the muzzles tkey wore as without them, as they just had a rope or a strap round their necks. • —The defendant was ordered to p 4. 2s. 6d., half the costs.

As OBNOXIOUS CRIPPLE. At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, Jonatpne Brown, a clippie, wag-charged with being drunk tieq ' disorderly in Mersey-st., on Saturday night, The pri- soner who has lost both his legs, is accustomed to traverse the streets seated in a small wheeled concern no bigger 'than a child's go-cart, which he propels by means of two sticks, begging of the passengers. Police-Sergeant Chantler said that prisoner was using most disgusting language to two persons in the street, and P.C. Rolling- worth corroborated him, and said the man was striking at people right and left with his stick. The prisoner did not belong to Warrington, and every time he came to the town he acted in a similar manner.—The prisoner said he was a poor helpless man, and he came intg the town on Friday, and paid ed. to lie on a stone floor.—The Mayor (addressing the prisoner) said he heard him mak- ing a big noise in Bridge-st. . He had no legs, but he had an extra amount of tongue.—The prisoner: Well, I was brought up a scholar.—He was discharged on promising to leave the town. THE MAYOR AND SELF-DEFENSIVE FISTICUFFS. At he Warrington Police Court on Monday, Samuel Thommasson, labourer at Houghton's wire works, of 21, Dale-st., Sankey Bridges, was charged with assaulting two young men unknown in Golden Square, on the night •of the 18th inst. P.C. 15, said the defendant, who was sober, knockedone of the men down and then turned round and struck the other. The defendant said the two men came up to him and said" This is him." He said "This is him; what for ?" and they would bot give him any answer. One of them knocked him down, and he (the defendant) retaliated by knocking his assailant down. The other man was coming for him and he bit him.—The Mayor observed to the deputy magistrates' clerk, who was addressing him at this moment, that he should be inclined to break the law himself if somebody attacked him in such a manner, and he told the defen- dant that the Bench (which now included himself and Mr. Sutton only. Alderman Harrison having left).thought he had only taken his part as any right-minded man man would do when attacked by:others. They did not wish him to do the same thing again, as another magis- trate migbt take a different view of such a case ; but under the circumstances, as the defendant bors a good character, they would give him the benefit of the doubt and discharge him. CHARGE OF FURIOUS DRIVITNTG.—A CONFLICT OF OPINION ON THE BENCH. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Friday, Benjamin Bryan was charged with furiously driving a horse and spring cart in Horsemarket-st., on the after- noon of AprillBth. A police-constable•said the defend- ant twice dropped the reins on to the horse's back, and allowed the animal tog. at such a rate that a bassinette, which was standing with one wheel on the parapet and one off was knocked over by the cart wheel, a child being thrown out of the perambulator. The tart ran into a 'bus horses' heads, and the 'bus driver bad to pull his horses off their fore feet • to prevent an accident. Another constable corroborated, and said defendant was driving at the rate of ten miles an hour.—Petsr Baguley, the 'bus driver, said the defendant was driving very fast, but, whether to avoid Witness's horses or not, he could not say. The child was thrown out of the preambulator, but not hurt, though the lady in charge of it was terribly upset.—The defendant said he only dropped his reins once, to get out of the way and prevent the 'bus running into witness's mare. The bassinette was nearly upset, not quite.—Mr. Bowcock, butcher, the defendant's employer, said the cart only half turned the perambulator over. If the de- fendant had not started the mare off as he did, there would have been a serious accident, and perhaps loss of life. The Chairman said there was a doubt in the case, and the Bench would give the defendant the benefit of it. Alderman Harrison said if he had been alone on the Bench he would have fined the defendant 40s. and cOsts.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman B. W. Francomb)
and Aldermen-Hairison and Sutton.

, DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Patrick Flattery and James Smith, in Bridge-st., on Saturday night, and John Bowes, in Wilderspool-road on Sanday morning, fined ss. each. Martin Brannan, in Pinner's Brow, on the 23rd inst.. and William Hill in Bridge-st., on the 22nd, discharged on payment of 6s. costs each.—Alfred Stokes, brought up under a warrant, for being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-road, on the 7th of February, had to pay 7s. 6d. DOGS AT LARGE USMUZZLED.—Ge'4rge Roberts, 59, Howley-lane, was charged with allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled in that thoroughfare on the 21st inst. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence. Three little girls gave evidence as tc the dog in question being in the street unmuzzled, the animal biting one of them and flying at another, but they were unable to prove that it was the defendant's dog; and, a police officer having -thrown further doubt on the case by his evidence, it was dismissed. THRowiNo sToNEs.—Patrick Donlan, 75, Stamford-st., Peter Lennon, Wm. Carroll, and Nicholas Warren were 'charged with throwing stones in Erwood-St. The con- stable who proved the case said they were throwing stoles through a broken pane in sonic property, having already broken one pane. Mr. H. Wood, of the firm of Messrs. Aslaton and Wood, solicitors, said within the last few months the whole of the glazing had been knocked out of some property for which they were agents. It had been put in again and boarded up, but the boards 'had been probed through and the windows broken in that way. Some stonework in a stable yard had been 'broken through, and the iron taken away; and a .lot of 'coping had been knocked off the wall. A large square of glass had been smashed, and three feet of spouting taken away.—The Mayor said the defendants would be fined 2s. 6d. each, and the police would have instruc- tions to try to catch all boys damaging property in the town; and such cases would be dealt with more Severely In future.—Me. Wood: Although the police'are only do- ting their dutv,we shall pay them a reward.—The Mayor: .hey ought to look after your interests without any re- 'ward; but we do not object if you wish to do it. CHIN YS ON FlRE.—Samuel Fernley. 14, liiankey-st., for having his chimney on fire on the 22nd April, was fined ls.-:—Thi).mas Colton, labourer, 17,West-st., for wil- fully setting his chimney on fire, he having done this for the purpose of cleaning it, was discharged on payment of the costs, 35. 6d.—Patrick Henley, 12, Stanley-st.. and John Stanley, 6, Orford-avenue, for allowing their chim- TIM to be on fire, were fined is. each. lioar-BALLINO IN VIE CharrlOCk,Fred.

Shaw. John Shaw, William Boyle Robert Fairbrother, and Thomas Ashton, for playing al football in Orchard- St., on April 22nd, were fined 2.5. fid. each. CARD-PLAYING FOR MONEY.—Patrick Ward, Michael Doyle, Thomas Lamb, and John Tyrell, for playing at cards for money, in Morris's-yard, on Sunday afternoon, were fined, Ward and Lamb ss. each, and the others 2s. 6d. each. NIGHT BICYCLING WITHOUT A LAMP.—Charles Fair- brother was charged with riding a bicycle in Orford- avenue, on the night of April 22nd, without having a lamp. P.C. Hollingworth said he had neither lamp nor bell. He was fined is.
TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. 1. Guest (in the chair) and W. Owen.

A SAVAGE OFFENDER.—CharIes Finch, a navvy, was charged on a warrant with having assaulted Joseph Woodini, landlord of the Legh Arms public house. It was stated that the prisoner was making a disturbance in the Legh Arms and had to be ejected. As he was be- irk ejected he bit Wooding on the hand, and caused a wound whieh had to be stitched by Dr. Fox. It was also said that Finch put his teeth into the waistcoat of the landlord's assistant. Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month's hard labour.—Mary Ann Finch, the wife of the last prisoner, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on the previous night. She pleaded guilty, and it was stated in evidence that it was believed she was on her way at the time of her apprehension to break the windows of the Legh Arms. She was fined ss. and costs.

A DISEASED lioa-ss.—William Dunbebbin was charged with having. on the 17th and 20th April, caused a horse, suffering from an infectious disease, to be taken along a thoroughfare. Evidence as to the diseased condition of the animal was given by Inspector Norman and Mr. Ferguson, veterinary surgeon. It was also deposed that defendant, who is in the employ of Mrs. Monks, rope- maker, on the two days named took the horse from the stable along the river side at Arpley, although he had been warned not to take it out till it was certified clear of disease. A tine of 10s. and costs was imposed. SCHOOL CASES.—Mr. George Riley prosecuted in the following cases, which were brought at the instance of the School Attendance Committee :—Charles Goldin, Old-road, fined ss. ; George Buckley, Ellesmere-st.. fined 2s. 6d.; John Billing, Latchford. fined 55.; Michael Carty, Philip-st., fined 55.; Thomas Moody, Catherine- at.; fined 55.; Edward Murray, Tanner's-lane, fined 55.; Mary Owen, Fennell-st. fined 2s. 6d.; Patrick Sheen- ing, School-brow, fineess. ; and Thomas Rushton, Hind- St., tined 53.—A warrant was issued in the case of Michael Flynn, Bewsey-road. . . .

ALLEGE]; 'hiErr OF A RASP.—Robert Miller, stone- mason, Orford-st., was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Orford-st. on the 22nd inst. ; also with stealing by means of a trick, a steel rasp, value is. 6d., from Mr. J. Chorley, Buttermarket-st.—Mr. Chorley stated that prisoner came into the warehouse and asked for a rasp, saying it was for Mr. Gittsns. Orford-st. The rasp was supplied to Miller, who gave no note, as was eustomary. Witness despatched a boy for a note to Mr. Gitteng, who replied that he had sent for no tool of any descriptiml.—Mr, °Wens also gave. evidence.—Prisoner said he had been working for Mr. ttens, and that he had bought the rasp on his own aceouht, And intended to pay for it.—For being drunk and disorderly prisoner was fined 10s. and costs, or in default 14 days' hard labour, and was given the benefit of the doubt on the charge of stealing. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes.

WILFUL DAMAGE TO A PLATE GLASS WINDOW.—John Thompson, printer, of no settled abode, was Charged with wilfully and maliciously damaging the plate glass window of the Pelican Vaults, Buttermaket-st., the property of John Allen, the prisoner doing damage to the amount of EL—P.C. Barnett said he saw the prisoner stand opposite the window, then turn round and push his left hand through it. He was sober. He was ordered to pay the damage and costs, or go to jail for a month.
TRIIRSDAY.—Before Major Pickmore (chairman) amid , Alderman Sutton.

AN INCORRIGIBLE ROGUE AND VAGABOND.—John Tomlin, labourer, was charged by Mr. Basil Shearer, on behalf of the Board of Guardians with leaving his children depen- dent on the Union, he being able to maintain them ; also with being a rogue and a vagabond. Mr. Shearer said the preference of the two charges was somewhat unusual, but under the Vagrancy Act Tomlid could be charged with neglecting to maintain himself, as well as not maintain- ing his children. Mr. Harbourne,relieving officer,stated that the defendant had, of his own accord, left the Ship Canal, where he was earning 4-4 d. an hour, and then brought his children into the Workhouse. He had been several times previously convicted,and was committed for trial to the Quarter Sessions as an incorrigible rogue and vagabond. INDECENT LANGUAGE.—IsabeIIa Fleming was charged under a warrant with Using indecent language on the 3rd of February. She was fined 10s. and costs, or fourteen days. FRlDAY.—Before Dr. White (chairman), Alderman Harrison, and Dr. Gornall.

Daunt AND DISORDERLY. Edward Cowen, drunk and disorderly the previous afternoon, in Rose Yard, was fined 55., including costs.—Julia Shields, for the like offence in Dial-st., on Thursday night, was sent to jail for a month. FRAUDULENT ENLISTMENT.—John Hayes or Barnes was charged with making a false answer on attestation on the 15th of March, when enlisting in the Liverpool Militia, by stating that he had formerly belonged to the Royal Lancashire militia. He was committed to prison fora month.

WOMEN'S QUARRELS.—Mary Ann Mannion was charged with assaulting Rebecca Riley on Monday night, in the Black Horse Inn. The complainant said she was singing there at the request of her husband who was with her,when Mr. Mannion who was with his wife,com- menced "throwing out hints "and using nasty langu- age. This led to a quarrel, and at length Mrs. Mannion struck the complainant in the face,and forced her mouth open with a key.—The defendant said the complainant "rung the place with singing." She struck her (the defendant) and pulled her hair off, knocking the zhild outof her arms .—The case was dismissed .—Bridget Cur- ley was charged with assaulting and beating Mary Hart on April 30th. The complainant stated that the defen- dant came to her house door in Stanley-st., while witness was standing at the top of the street, and knocked at the door with a poker. Then Wm. Curley came and started knocking. She said there was no one in and then both he r and the defendant assaulted her.—The defendant said the complainant struck her with a teapot, and she had to go the Infirmary.—The complainant said the Curleys broke into two lodging-houses of which she and her husband bac:l4 charge and with which their private house was connected. A female witness stated that the Curleys knocked the latch off the door and that Wm. Curlew struck the com- plainant, and told her he would fight her husband or her brother. Witness afterwards saw Wm. Curley all over blood, fighting with one of Mrs. Hart's lodgers. The de- fendant struck Mrs. Hart three times, and witness did not see Mrs. Hart strike Mrs. Curley with a teapot.—Mrs Ceilings said Wm. Curley when he went to the door said he .wanted to fight the lodger.—The defendant was bound over in her own recognisatices to keep the peace for 6 months, and ordered to pay the costs us. MORE STREET FournAtuNo.—John Armitage, John Cunningham, John Forster, James Forster, and William Rutter, four of them being of the " hobbledehoy " class, and two of them boys were charged with beinc, dis- orderly by playing at football in Finnees Brow, on April 29th. P.C. Direacock said the ball went against the frame of a plate glass window, but did not break the window. They were fined 2s. 6d. and costs each.

DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TIIESDAY.—Before Messrs. Eiward Greenall (chairman), C. Parr, Wm. Long, H. Neild, and J. Marson. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.--SITOUTING EXTRAORDINARY. —Henry Clayton, labourer, of Appleton, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on the highway on the 19th inst. Sergeant Booth said the defendant's shouts could be heard a quarter of a mile away. He was fined ss. and costs, 9s. 6e. in all. A DRUNKEN CAB DRIVER.—John Jackson, a cab driver, of Runcorn, was charged with being drunk on the high- way while in charge of a horse and cab,at Walton,on the 4th April. P.C. Shatwell proved the case. He said he was sitting in his lodgings at Higher Walton, and saw the defendant drive to the Walton Arms. He was drunk and witness went to him and told him he would not allow him to take the cab away as he was not in a tit condition to be in charge of it. A man who was in the cab said he would take the horsd to the stables, and witness allowed him to do so. This being the defend- ant's first offence, he was discharged on payment of 2s. 6d. costs.
KEEPING A DOG WITHOUT A LICENSE.—Peter Hill, of Acton Grange, for keeping a dog without a license, was mulcted in the costs:-

ABSENTEES FROM SCHOOL.-401111 Miller, of Stretton, and Joseph Arnold, of Wilderspool, were fined ss. each, including costs, for not sending their children to school. William Henry Owrn was summoned for neglecting to send his eon and daughter to school. The mother ap- peared, and said she had kept the girl from school, but not the boy, except on one day, as she had sent him "seventeen half-days" to school and each time the mas- ter had sent enim back for the fee, 3d., though she owed nothing for fees. Mr. De Prez, the School Attendance Officer, who prosecuted in this and the preceding school cases, said if the master allowed a child to remain in school without paying the fees he could not recover them in any court, and if the defendant's wife's excuse were accepted there Would be no children at school,—The de- fendant was fined 55., including, costs, in each case.— Charles Delooze was charged with not complying with an order dated Dec. 30th4 to send his child to Stockton Heath School. ,The defendant's wife appeared,and said the lad played truant. The Bench desired to know if she ob- jectedgent to an industrial school, and she repliedttohialatvse hlhedrild, but did not object to his being sent to the training ship Clio. The Magistrates' Clerk said that was an industrial school, not a reformatory. The Bench fined the defendant 55., including costs, and told the woman that if the lad's Case were brought up again an order would be made for his being sent away. The Magistrates' Clerk: You say you don't want the child sent to an industrial school. This is giving you an op- portunity of keeping him at home.
7-- RUNCORN"; PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas. TRANSFER.—WiIIiam Martin Williams was granted
temporary authority to sell at the Mariner's Hotel, Per- cival-lane, under the license granted to John George Halstead.

BREACN OF CANAL BOATS ACT.—Charles Scragg, cap- tain of the canal boat Umbria! belonging to the Anderton Company, was summoned by the Runcorn Board of Com- missioners, for having on the 6th April allowed the cabin of the boat, which was used as a sleeping place to ne occupied by a certain other person of female sex, above the age of 12 years contrary to the Canal Boats Act. The defendant pleaded guilty, and Mr. Boote, inspector of canal boats, proved the case. A representative from the Anderton Company, said the cabin was divided by shutters, and the defendant did not know he was break- ing the law.—The Bench ordered the defendant to pay the costs 12s. 6d.
CARD PLAY.—John Waterworth, a labourer, was charged with gaming by playing cards at the Stone Hills. —P.C. 59, proved the case and a fine of 2s. 6d. and costs 9s. 6d. was inflicted.

STONE THROWING ON No MAN'S LAND.—A boy. named Frederick Drinkwater (11), was summoned by John Ingham, an old soldier, for assaulting him.—lngham said on the 17th April he was on duty at the level cross- ing on No Man's Land. There were about 14 boys there, and he drove them away. They commenced to throw, stones, and the defendant struck him on the wrist and on the breast with stones. The other boys threw care- lessly, but defendant meant mischief. The defendant denied that he had thrown, and he was dismissed on pay- ing the costs ss. ed. SCHOOL BOARD CASES.—Several parents were sum- moned for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual fine of ss. was imposed in each case.

Sampson received the oval and intended it for Potts, but Hurst got clear and changed the venue to the Warrington quarter. A pass- ing movement between Thomas, Gwynn, and McCut- cheon saw the latter being well tackled over the line, but he managed to ground, and a clever try was the result. 2ennington took the place, and luck was with Oldham, for the oval struck both uprights and then bounded through. Not in the least disheartened lfy this reverse the Warringtonians entered the fray with renewed exer- tions, and although Hurst effected a fine run for Oldham, a bout of passing between Davies, Catterall, and Barnes saw the Warrington centre putting in a run, dodging in and out as he proceeded, until he had cleared all opposi- tion, and then the effect began to tell on him,and Gwynn, catching him near the line, just managed to pull him up This was a brilliant run, and well merited the applause which greeted it. From some loose play, Davies got over behind the posts, but the point was over-ruled. Boscow responded to a kick by Gwynn, and the oval was on the Oldham line whencthe whistle sounded half-time, the score reading as—Warrington 0-0-1, Oldhatn, 1-0-0. Warrington restarted, and from a free kick in the first minute, Sampson had a shot at goal, but the kick was short. Hurst foolishly ran the oval out, and his side were penned for a considerable period after this. Barnes narrowly missed scoring on two occasions, and Penning- ton brought relief in the nick of time, when a tall kick took the game to the half way Ag.g. Some stnart play by the Oldham forwards eventusAly reached the War- rington line, but 'Ashton, Povey, Berry, and Donohue hai the oval back again, and Barnes,obliging with one of his characteristic runs, again threatened the h?me goal. A penalty kick to each side was the next item, and from the one taken by Hurst, Boscow saved. Berry, Russell, and Povay dribbled well, and play was of a more vigorous kind. Catterall passed wildly when the 'Oldham goal was at the mercy of his colleagues, and Sampson was severely tried on the popular side, and although he mis- judged the oval on many occasions, he managed to field the ball grandly afterwards and kick exceptionally well when in difficulties. Fine play by Lally, Berry,Donohne. and Ashton neutralised sonie passing by Gray and Thomas, and although Hurst made big mark, Boscow responded in true style,and the home goal was menaced. Pretty passing between Lally, Speakman, and Barnes deserved a better fate, but towards the close the War- ringtonians put on pressure, and their forwards being masters of the situation the oval was rushed over in the last minute, and Russell was credited with having scored a well-earned try. Barnes failed at a somewhat easy place, and the final result was as follows: Warrington„ 0-1-1 ; Oldham, 1-0-1. Teams :—Warrington : J. BO3COW, back; Potts, Barnes and Sampson, three-quarters; Lally and Speak- man, half backs; Ashton, Holmes, Berry, Donohue, Povey, Davies, Teare' Russell, Catterall, forwards. ST. HELENS V. RUNCORN (2Eld teams) —These teams met at St. Helens on Saturday and the match resulted in a win for St. Helens by one goal, one try, and five minors to Runcorn one try and two minors. RuNcomi v. WIDNES. A match between these two clubs was played at Runcorn, on Saturday, before a large number ot spectators the gate being equally divided. Faulkner kicked off and Eludes returred well, and scrim- maging commenced in the neighbourhood of the Widnes half. A pretty piece of passing between Hughes, Faulk- ner, May, and Wainwright was promptly nipped by Plumpton before any mischief had been wrought. Fol- lowing up with great persistence, Widnes worked their way into Runcorn territory, but while the Runcorn pack were getting the worst of it, the backs were playing beautifully together,and the splendid passing and kicking of the wearers of the green neutralized all attempts to lower their goal. With the game in the Widnes 25, Faulkner gave Davies a pass which the three-quarter took in his usual style, and,dodging Plumpton beautifully,got almoo on the line, when he was tackled. From a line out Hughes passed to Alv, who transferred tO Davies, and the latter dodging a Couple cf adversaries, 'got op- posite the goal and cleverly dropped the oval over the bar, amid enthusiastic cheers. Resuming from the centre, Widnes began to assume an aggressive movement, and, a punt by Barber sending the leather over the Run- corn line, Houghton touched down. A second minor for Widnes was registered through a drop at goal by Plump- ton, and after a few minutes more of even play, Plump- ton's kicking accomplishments forced the third minor and brought on half-time, with the score a dropped goal for Runcorn, and three minors for Widnes. The second half-hour of the warfare was opened by Smith, and the initial phases were advantageous to his side, but the selfishness of Brennan was so palpable and so short- sighted that much of the attacking force was thwarted. A smart bit of following up by Davies gained a lot of ground, which was quickly recovered when the Widnes forwards got to work, and for a short time the ball travel- led rapidly between the quarter flag. A splendid dribble by P. Riley was well neutralized by Plumpton. A short struggle near the line ended in Gordon kicking the leather over the line and forcing Wain/right to touch down. Still Widnes pressed, and if the men had only been smart enough, there were plenty of opportunities for scoring. Nothing further was scored, and the match terminated in a win for Runcorn by a dropped goal to five minors for Widnes. The following were the teams :—Runcorn: S. Houghton, full back ; T. H. Davies, H. May, and G. T. Wainwright. three-quarters; H. Hughes and W. Faulk- ner, half-backs; P. Riley, J. Gayter, A. Hampson, P. Dolan, W. Shaw, 0. Hughes, H. Williams, G. Leigh, and T. Derbyshire, forwards. Widnes: J. Hartles, full back ; F. Plumpton, D. Brennan, and H. Peters, three-quarters; H. Barber and J. Drummond, half backs; J. H. Smith, G. Hewitt, A. Lyons, J. Whelan, R. Ridgway, J. Johnson, J. Hardman, C. Emery, and E. Gordon, forwards. Re, feree, Mr. J. Ashton. WARRINGTON "A " v. OLDHAM "A."—The last match of the season between these rivals was fought on the Warrington ground, on Saturday. The game was started by the home team, and a raid by Barnes, Buckley, and Lawless was at once made, and Oldham to avoid disas- ter touched down. Amovement by Thorne and Isher- wood took the leather to the visitOrs' 25, where Beaver, intercepting a pass, ran to midfield. The oval was not destined to remain here long, for strong rushes by Hackett, Bailey, Knowles, and Molyneaux forced a second minor. Although the kick out was of no advant- age, Watkin cleared his lines finely, but from subsequent proceedings, Nevins ran splendidly through the whole ruck, and owing te a mistake 4 try was thrown away, and only a minor accrued, another quickly following. Oldham now played up, and were soon about the home quarter flag, and some passing between Beaver and Mc- Donnell sent the ball dead. Thornley showed up very prominently after this, and although a fine kick by Beaver drove Warrington back, Buckley, Knowles, and Barnes cleared the impending danger, and Bailey throw- ing to Heesom, thE latter's kick found touch at the Old- ham 25. Some loose play, in which Isherwood, Cragan, and Molyneaux indulged, wa.yesponded to by Kershaw, but Lawless passing to Mather, the last-named ran splen- didly to the line, and Barnes scored, Heesom placing the goal. Restarting, Thornley was notable for a run, and after passing by Knowles, Mather, and Heesom, the lat- ter ran prettily to the quarter, Buckley directly after dashing over the line, Heesom again converting. Going with a rush, Oldham visited the homesters' territory, but retaliation on the part of Bailey, Hackett, and Thornley carried the sphere to neutral territory, where Hackett, who had been playing in grand style, got hurt, and had to retire. After this another flying visit by Oldham was made until driven to the half-way by Lawless. Effective play by Beaver made matters look black, but Knowles, Molyneaux, Cragan, and Bailey nipped the attack in the bud, and half time was called with Warrington two goals ahead. Resuming, a fine bit of work by Mather caused pressure to bear. until Beaver and Bennett ran and passed to the Warrington territory, and Oldham at- tacked vigorously. Nevins relieved grandly, but a long, kick sent the ball dead. Thornley's kick gained con- siderably, and some pretty play by Heesom was neutra- lized by a rush. After Nevins had again been prominent, the visitors lost a fine chance by bad passing, but a fine run by Simpson almost had the desired result. Buckley nullified by a strong rush, and transfers between Lawless and Mather enabled the latter to get away to the half- way line. A fine dribble, headed by Knowles, Thornley, and Molyneaux, improved the situatiop, and a long kick by Plinston found the leather dodging near the line, Heesom almost dropping a goal. -Dropping out, Oldham dashed away, only to find Nevins driving them back grandly. A neat bit of passing between 'leaver, Ker- shaw, and Bennett was the next item, the ground being soon regained by Knowles's flue dribble,and being supple- mented by a run from Cragan, the visiting lines were in danger. Hamblett was afterwards called upon, and following some rough and tumble struggles, the ball was again at the Oldham end, Knowles dodging over the line, the whistle blowing with Warrington 2-1-5 to Oldham 0-0-2.

div.head: WARRINGrTON v. OLDHAM.
div.p: WARRINGrTON v. OLDHAM.

Oldham have not experienced the best of luck in their fixtures with Warrington during the last three years, for either fog or frost have put a damper on the matches, and Oldham have consequently been robbed of one of their best gates. Frost stopped the match of the now past season, but the Warrington Executive came to the rescue of the Oldham Committee, and it was arranged that the Warringtonians should visit the Watersheddings enclo- sure last Saturday. The response to the appeal fer the benefit of the homesters was indeed a hearty one, and it was estimated that over 5,000 lined the ropes. Some dis- appointment was felt at the Warringtonians having a somewhat scratch combination, and the general opinion was formed that Oldham would win, and that easily. But the unexpected was in store, and the substitutes who acced in place of Evans, the two Bates, the Brothers Turner, Nevins, Jolley, and Randles, playing for every- thing they were worth, upset calculations, and Warring- ton at the close were a ,trifie unlucky in not gaining the day.

Oldham were without Whittaker, and losing the toss, Gwynn kicked off, Potts making no reply. From the scrimmage at the Warrington quarter flag, Donohue dribbled to half-way ere he was checked by Gray, but a combined piece of play between Lally and Potts took play on the Oldham line, and, contrary te expectation, the Warringtonians kept up the attack. Repeated en- deavours to clear were made by McCutcheon, Thomas, and Hurst, but our local team were on their mettle and never allowed them to travel far. Barnes easily accounted for Gwynn, and some bad play by the Oldham three- quarters terminated in a minor being conceded the visi- tors. A fine run by McCutcheon was promptly neutra- lized by Sampsan, who got in his kick under difficulties, and Holmes with an individual dribble reached the home quarters, but Nuttall and Thomas in response gave the Oldham men a glimpse of the Warrington goal. The visitors had a warm time of it now, scrimmage succeed- ing scrimmage for the space of five minutes, until at last Barnes,foiling Gwynn,dribbled down the open, and being aided by some kicking on the part of Sampson and Bos- cow, the homesters again had to defend. Teare and Russell were especially prominent with some fine

WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION V. GRAMMAR SCHOOL. These teams tried conclusions for the tfirst time on the ground of the latter. The visitors were without the ser- vices of Ball, Onions (injured), Parry, and Jones. The visitors kicking off rather late, the school hac.'l the bene- fit of the opening exchanges, and were rather dangerous for the first ten minutes, but the visitors settling down t 8 their work transferced the operations towards the home goal, Carter hitting the posts with a good shot. The Association continued the attack, but owing to the wretched shooting display were unable to score, half- time arriving with a clean sheet. Restarting the home right were noticeable for some fine runs, but founa Mather and Davies too much for them. An attack on the home goal by Powell and T. Mather ended in the school backs relieving but only to be again assailed by Clayton and Cornforth, but to no purpose, the backs and goalkeeper playing an excellent defensive game. Even- tually, after several futile attempts, Clayton got in a splendid shot which scored the only goal for the match, thus ending a poor game with Warrington Association 1 goal, Grammar School none. The visitors played a poor game all round, not one of them showing anything like their usual form, while as to the school they had the making of a good team the right wing pair being very good, as also is the back division. Warrington team : Goal, Warburton; backs, Phillips and Davies; half backs, Aylina (capt.), Carter. J. Mather; forwards, Clayton, Martin, Cornforth, T. Mather, and Powell. Referee, Mr. Dixon.

DISASTER TO OPERATIC AMATEURS.
TWO. YOUNG LADIES KILLED

NEw Yonx, THURSDAY.—A sad calamity is reported from Troy, Alabama. As a party of young people were rehearsing an amateur performance in the Opera House, on Wednesday, the building collapsed. The roof, which was one of a terge span, was intended to be of a self supporting character, but owing, it is alleged, to faulty construction, it suddenly fell in, burying twenty of the children under a mass of girders woodwork, and other materials. The crash, which was terrific, alarmed the whole neighbourhood. Assistance was soon at haad,and the unfortunate people were extricated from their terrible position. It was, however, found that two young ladies Miss Foster and Miss Starke, had been killed, while two others were seriously injured. The remaining sixteen were also injured, but not seriously.
LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUIiCIL AND TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION.

On Wednesday night Vie report of the Technical Instruction Committee of the Lancashire County Council was issued from the County Offices,Preston. In pursuance of the resolution passed at the last meeting of the County Council, the Committee has appointed Mr. Lloyd Evans to inquire into every application for a grant. The Committee beg to re- commend that for industrial technical instruction grants in aid be made to the following: 1. To classes associated with the Science and Art Department, the City and Guilds of London Institute, and other institutions and schools, if the subjects taught come within the Technical Instruction Acts, such grants to depend, to a great extent, on the number of students and the result of the examinations. 2- To classes for teaching domestic science to women. 3. For univer- sity extension lectures on subjects covered by the Tech- nical Instruction Acts; the conditions on which such Igrants are to be made to be hereafter defined. 4. To technical schools in country boroughs, taking into con- sideration the number of students attending such schools from tke administrative county. 5. To foimd trevelling scholarships, to assist attendance at tech- nical school at at a distance. 6. To found schola- ships at the Liverpool and Manchester colleges, in connnection with the Victoria University, on conditions to be hereafter arranged. 7. To central colleges, institu- tions, and sc,hools, for the purpose of educating teachers. 8. That a sum not exceeding £5OO be granted for the purpose of assisting the formation of migratory dairy schools in such agricultural centres as would aid in their establishment by providing premises, appliances, and other facilities for work. 9. That a further sum not exceeding L 2.50 be granted for providing a movable wooden building. 10. That District Committees be ap- pointed, if necessary, for defined areas, such District Committees to consist partly of members of the County Council. 11. That the Committee here-appointed, with ower to carry out the above recommendations.
THE ARCHDEACON'S VISITATION TO WARRINGTON.

At the Warrington Parish Chinch, on Wednesday Dr. Taylor, Archdeacon of Warrington, delivered his charge to the churchwardens and sidesmen of the Archdeaconry of Warrington. who were then ad- mitted to their offices. Previous to the address of the Archdeacon, a short service was conducted by the Rector (the Rev. F. W. Willis). In the course of his charge, Archdeacon Taylor referred to the duties of churchwardens. Briefly,those duties were to provide, or see provided, the things necessary for the decent and reverent performance of Divine worship; to take care of the sacred building, and see that it was maintained in proper repair and cleanliness; and to provide for the comfort ani con- venience of worshippers. In respect to seating,the wardens had not an arbitrary authority,but the law would protect them in the exercise of a reasonable' discretion for the benefit and comfoit of the whole congregation in directing individuals where to sit. The office was one of observation and complaint if necessary, but not one of direct control over the ser- vices or the conduct of the minister in reference thereto. It had been thought by many that it would be well if they had more control in this matter, but they had only to deal with the law as it stood and not as they thought it should be. , In everything concerning the services ofithe church the minister alone was responsible, and all the wardens could do was, at the proper time and in the manner pre- scribed by law, to present matters complained of in due form to the bishop. He invited serious attention to the subject of finance, more especially with reference to the stipends of the clergy, which was not a matter on which the clergy would not speak for themselves. In these days of shrinking tithes and diminishing pew rents it should not be overlooked, and he appeared for reasonable provision for the ministers of the Church, suggesting a revival of the practice of having at Easter an offertory for the sole benefit of the minister. In such a movement the initiative should come from the wardens. There was at present a strong outcry against seat rents for this purpose, and it was sometimes maintained that it was absolutely and in every case illegal. That was a great mistake. In old parish churches, no doubt they were illegal, but in all churches erected under the Church Building Acts, 1 and 2 Vic., 58 and 59, and George 111., 1819, if not even from the 43rd, George, 1803, to Lord Blandford's Act, 19 and 20, Vic., 1856, they were expressly legalised, under the discretion of the Ecclesias- tical Commissioners, who were authorised to fix a scale of pew rents, of course under the sanction of the ordinaries. His impression was that in this matter a hard and fast rule c•ould not be laid down for all cases, but in churches in large towns, in his opinion, the accom- modation should be as free as possible. Having advocated support of the Diocesan Sustentation Fund, the Arch- deacon, speaking of the means that had been adopted to raise income, said that in one of the returns he had read with sincere regret the mention of a ball. He said nothing about the holding of balls in the abstract— he had nothing to do with them ; they were not in his line—but it was not seemly, to say the least,that such a method should be resorted to for the purpose of defray- ing the necessary expenses of divine worship in God's house. Balls were not a proper method of Church fin- ance, and it was not one to which the Church of Christ should be indebted. He would rather go from house to house amongst the parishioners, than resort to such methods. The Church of Christ should not be indebted to the ball room. In six cases the wardens presented that there was not sufficient church accommodati3ll, but he believed the deficiency would soon be made up. On Saturday the Bishop consecrated the 29th church within the last ten years, and others were in process of erectien. In conclusion, he pointed out that supreme power in regard to national affairs had passed into the hands of the people, and no institution would be allowed to escape the most searching and perhaps even hostile criticism. The National Church could not claim exemp- tion from this ordeal, and sooner or later would be called upon to justify its existence as such. Let him impress upon them to do all in their power to exercise an influence to preserve their grand old national historic Church, walking in the old paths, resting on the old foundations, and not allowing to be removed the inde- pend ant landmarks that our fathers set up.—The church- wardens and sidesmen were then admitted.

THE INFLUENZA AGAIN.
DEATH AT PONTEFRACT.
I
At Bolton several hundreds of persons have been at- tacked, though no deaths are reported at present. There are numerous cases at Spalding, Gosberton, and in the south county.

In Ashton-under-Lyne there are hundreds of cases, and great inconvenience to business is being caused. In Chesterfield the same condition of affairs prevails. At Leeds, exactly one-half of the telegraph messengers are off duty, and at Bradford several deaths are reported. Mr. Mundella is a sufferer, having been confined to bed since Saturday.

An outbreak of Influenza is reported in Liverpool,many cases having occurred during the past fortnight. In Birkenhead a similar phenomenon has been noted. In Lincolnshire the malady continues to spread alarmingly, and at Huddersfield several deaths have occurred. The Master of the Stockport Union Workhouse on Monday reported a serious outbreak in the institution under his care.

Thomas Havester, of Beech-grove, Pontefract, who was married on Good Friday. died on Saturday from the effects of a severe attack of influenza. The epidemic affected him mentally as-well as physically. On Sunday William Roberts, a youth residing at Tanshelf, died from the same disease. On Monday morning Sergeant O'Leary of the York and Lancashire Regiment, died in Pontefract Barracks, having succumbed to a similar attack. Alto- gether some 400 cases of influenza are known to exist in Pontefract.

div.head: MOLTKE.
div.p: MOLTKE.

Field Marshal Count Moltke died on Friday evening, in •kis ninety-first year. He had attended the sitting of the Reichstag during the day,and he was spending the even- ing as usual at home', listening to music and playing a rubber, when he felt unwell. He went to bed, and soon -afterwards passed away peacefully.

At the opening of Saturday's sitting of the Lower House of the Prussian Diet, the President, in communi- cating to the House the news of Count Von Moltke's death, said—The high value of the deceased's services to our fatherland, and the universal mourning which will be felt throughout Germany at his loss, convince me that the House will not desire to proceed with the business on the order of the day. I therefore pi opose an adjourn- ment until Monday next. The proposal was unani- mously agreed to, and the sitting was raised imme- diately. In the Upper House. where a laurel wreath, inter- twined with ribbons of black and white satin, hung over the seat usually occupied by the late Count, the Presi- dent, after reading a letter from Major Moltke, announc- ing the Field Marshal's death, delivered an address, in which he referred to the late Count's merits, and to the services rendered by him in his capacity as member of the Upper House. The House subsequently adjourned until Monday as a mark of respect to the memory of the great soldier.

• HIS CAREER. Count Hellmuth von Moltke, Chief Marshal of the German Empire, Chief of the General Staff, was des- cended (says "Men of the Time ") from a well-known Mecklenburg family, and was born at Parchim, October 26th, 1800, in the neighbourhood of which place his father, a famous officer of the Mollendorf Regiment, pos- sessed the estate of Gueritz. Soon after Hellmuth's birth his parents settled down in Holstein; and thus the boy, in his twelfth :year, went to Copenhagen, in order to devote himself, in the barracks there, to the military profession. In 1822 he entered the Prussian service as a lieutenant in the Bth Infantry Regiment, and studied in the Military Academy. The war had nearly ruined his parents, and the young officer was thrown entirely on his own resources. After having spent some time in the School of Division of Frankfort-on-the-Oder, Moltke was entered into the General Staff. In 1835 he undertook a tour in Turkey, which brought him under the notice of the Sultan Mamoud, who advised with the young Prus- sian officer on there-organization of the Turkish Army. Moltke remained several years in Turkey. and in 1839 Stook part in the campaign of the Turks in Syria against the Viceroy Mehemed Ali of Egypt, and his adopted son. Ibrahim Pasha. In 1845, having returned to Prussia,and Published an account of his Turkish experiences, he be- I came adjutant to Prince Henry of Prussia, then resident in Rome, and after his death, in 1847 Was engaged in connection with the general corn- , Mand on the Rhine, becoming in 1848, a member of the Grand General Staff, and in 1849 Chief of the Staff of 1 the 4th Army Corps in Magdeburg. In 1858 he was ad- vanced to the rank of Chief of the Grand General Staff of , the Prussian Army, and in 1859 became a lieutenant- , o general. In the Austro-Italian war Moltke was present in the Austrian headquarters. After the conclusion of Peace he spared no pains that he might fully develop the 'capacities of the Prussian General Staff and the Prus- sian Army. When the war of 1864 against Denmark broke out, Moltke sketched the plan of the campaign, and assisted in its execution, acting similarly in the War of 1866. The whole plan of the Bohemian campaign was due to the Lieutenant-General, whoa was personally Present in the battle of Konigratz, which he led, and in like manner arranged the bold advance of Prussian columns against Olsoutz and Vienna, and negotiated the armistice and tiae preliminaries of peace. For these ser- vices he receidtd the order of the Black Eagle and a national donation. To "Father Moltke" (Vater Moltke), as he was familiarly termed in the German army, and his brilliant strategy are ascribed the splendid victories of the German arms in the Franco-German War. He was Practically the Commander-in-Chief. The whole plan of the campaign was duo to him. In recognition of his un- rivalled services, Moltke was made the Chief Marshal of the Gorman Empire (September, 1871), again received a national donation, and was created Count in 1872. The illustrious Marshal, who was generally regarded as the first strategist of the day, received from the Czar the Order of St. George, the highest 'military decoration of Russia. in October 1870 ; and from his own Sovereign the Grand Cross of the Order of the iron Cross, March 22, 1871. An English translation of his " Observations on the influence that arms of precision have on modern tac- tics "was published in London 1871. THE EMPEROR AND THE MARSHAL. BERLIN, SATURDAY AFTERNOON.—This mourning over the death of Field-Marshal Von Moltke is universal and genuine. Thousands of people exhibit crape, and flags are at half-mast on all private, as well as public buildings. As soon as the Emperor William heard of the sad event he started for Berlin after sending a short' telegram of condolence, in which he said that he had lost one who was more to Germany than an entire army corps. The Empress proceeded to the official residence of the deceased, and expressed to the bereaved relatives her deep sympathy with them in their loss, adding that the whole country and the Royal House mourned with them. Before leaving the Empress was conducted into the death chamber, and gazed for a moment or two on the placid features of the dead warrior. After her Majesty's departure, Professor Lessing took a plaster cast of the face. MESSAGE FROM PRINCE BISMARCK. Berlin bade farewell for ever to Count Moltke on Tues- day. The coffin was closed early in the morning, and a funeral service was held at the General Staff Building. The Emperor, the King of Saxony,.the Grand Dukes of. Baden, Hesse, and Saxe-Weimar, and a large number of the princes of Germany stood before the catafalque in the Conference Hall. The sermon was preached by the Chaplain General of the Forces; and the Emperor dur- ing the whole ceremony wept bitterly. Troops of all arms were drawn up round the Column of Victory and along the route to the station. Prince Bismarck, who Was invited like all the Knights of the Black Eagle, was absent from the last honours paid to the man without Whom his diplomacy would have met with no success. Sir Edward Malet;the British Ambassador, represented the Queen. An immense arrived from Prince Bismarck, who also sent the following telegram :—" With profound sorrow I received telegraphic communication of the irreparable loss sustained by the Fatherland. I feel this loss the More acutely owing to its having been voUchsafeti to me to enjoy for many decades not only the Field Marshal's glorious co-operation in the service,but also the invariable amiability which he displayed in the close and friendly relations which I had the honour to maintain with him." INTERMENT AT KREISAU. KREISAU, WEDNESDAY.—The train conveying the re- mains of the late Count Von Moltke from Berlin, arrived here at two o'clock this afternoon. The coffin was con- veyed from the station to the mausoleum by twelve non- ilommissioned officers of the Great Elector's Cuirassier Regiment, who was relieved in turn by twelve officers of the 38th Infantry of the Line. The notabilities await- ing on the platform included General Levinski, Dr. Kopp, Prince-Bishop of Breslau and the civil and military authorities. The road from the station to the mausoleum 'was lined by the Veteran Societies. The coffin was fol- lowed to the wave by numerous deputations and a con- siderable crowd, including the inhabitants of Kreisau. Pastor Schiro Gruedity delivered a funeral oration at the grave, and the ceremony, which lasted only half-an- hour, commenced and concluded with the singing of an anthem.
THE BLACKGUARDISM OF STOCKTON
HEATH YOUTHS.

At the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Mr. J. Whitley, shopkeeper, of Stockton Heath, said at the request of some of the respectabhi inhabitants of that district, he appeared before the magistrates to complain that from the hour of half-past eight till about eleven at night they were very much annoyed by improper language used by youths standing about their business premises, and collect- ing in the neighbourhood. They cursed and swore, and used the most objectionable language.—The Chairman: lave you applied to the police P—Mr. Whitley: They inform me they have not got the same laws to prevent it as there are in force in the borough of Warrington.— The Chairman said the Bench had no power to deal with such offenders.—Mr. Whitley said there was a lady living in the neighbourhood who was severely afflicted, and it ,N'as i,ery distressing to her to hear the language used by these youths, who came round about on the footpaths. They did nothing but insult him when he spoke to them. The Magistrates' Clerk: All the police can do is to ask. them to move.—Mr. Whitley.. said they watched the Police and knew when they came. There was no com- Plaint ap to the police at all.—The Magistrates' Clerk explained that though such conduct could be dealt with '33 law in boroughs, country districts did not come under the act.—Mr. Whitley assured the Bench that life as becomina. unbearable to inhabitants of Stockton Reath through the nuisance, and now when the long e_venings were coming it would be worse.--Supekinten- sa_ent Large promised the magistrates that the police hould do all in their power to put an end to it.

MEETING OF WARRINGTON FUSTIAN CUTTERS.

• On Monday evening a meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall, Winwick-st., for the purpose of explaining to the fustian cutters of Warrington the benefits of membership of the Northern Counties Weavers', Reelers', Winders', Female Warpers', and Fustian Cutters' Association. Amongst those on the platform were Messrs. A. Buckley (secretary of the Association), J. Hayes, and J. Parnell. Mr. Stringer of Manchester, presided. There was-a fair attend- ance of persons employed in the fustian cutting shops of the town. The CHAIRMAN said that the fustian cutters of Man- chester and Salford, and some other places, had already joined the Association and it was the Manchester and Salford cutters who had subscribed the money for getting up that meeting. By joining the Uhion the fustian cut- ters of Warrington would be in a stronger position than they were in now, and would be able to get more of their rights. There was not a man or a woman in that room who worked at the frame, got their fair share of the money the masters got from the warehouses. Yet they were in no position to compel the masters to give them any more, but if they joined that Union they would have both funds and clever leaders behind them. (Ap- plause.) Mr. A. Buckley said he was only sorry the fustian cut- ters of Warrington had not seen the utility of organising themselves before now. If they had, their position would not have been what it was that night. In that district, owing to the want of combination, they were working for prices far below those paid in his neighbou hood, and they were debarring others from going in for an advance of wages. (Hear, hear). If they missed that opportunity of combining they would probably have to remain in a state .that he called slavery. He was told they had been promised or had got last week an increase of is., but if they did not combine what guarantee ,liad they that the shilling would remain? (" We haven't got it yet.") It was known that that meeting was going to he held, and the shillipg had simp- ly been put on to quieten a number of the cutters in the town. The dodge had been tried before. (Hear, hear). He believed there were men in Warrington who would willingly give a rise of wages if the biggerfry would only start. They knew how some of the small:ir employes were placed, and that tactics could be used that would drive them out of the market. The result was that, let them be ever so desirous to better the position of tbeir workpeople, they were deterred from doing so, for fear the men who had plenty of monerwould shove tuem out into the cold. That state of things could be altered by organisation, if they had the desire to organise. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They had a state of things going on in Warrington which he could hardly believe when he first heard of it. He referred to the apprentice system. He had seen children that day who promised to be first-class cutters, but what were they getting for their work? They were bound hand and foot, The slaves ot the Southern States of America used to be better off than these poor people were. The slaves were at all events properly clothed and properly fe,d, but he was afraid it would be very painful to go into the houses of some of the poor people he referred to and see their bill of fire. It could not be otherwise because of the small .amount of money they were paid. And who were the gainers by this state of things? They were men who ought to be more humane, and who ought to look more to the well-being of those under their charge. He was afraid that, generally speaking, so long as they could roll along in their carriages, they did not give the matter a thought; all they cared for was getting the money. (Applause.) The speafer then went on to refer to the advantages .of being connected with a Trades Union. The Union he represented, he said, had a membership of 50,000, and had just that day been successful in a eouple of severe strikes, one at Leigh and and the other at Todmorden. If the fustian cutters of Warrington would only enrol themselves in the Union he thought he might prophesy that, before many weeks were over,they would go home with more " brass " every time they cut a piece than they , did now. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.)

1 The CHAIRMAN having explained some of the rules of the Society, the sense of the meeting was taken as to the advisability of organising the fustian cutters of the town. Judging from a show of hands, much the greater part of the meeting appeared to be in favour of organisa- tion. Arrangements having been made for the enrolling of names, the meeting terminated.

MTh JOHN PEERS AND SCIENCE. Sir,—ln reply to Mr. John Peers, I must say that I took what I *then regarded, and what I still regard, as the most reasonable, if not charitable, construction of his letter, Mr. 'John Peers must rkeforget that he classed Newton and Herschel together as being "uninfluenced" by the disturbing influences of geology and biology. But if Newton remained uninfluenced, the same cannot be said of Herschel, for he lived while these influences were in lull sway. Accordingly, instead of clearing himself, Mr. John Peers seems to me to plunge more deeply into difficulties, and to impose himself as much as ever to the charge of" darkest ignorance" regarding Herschel.— am lac. April 38th, 'lB9l.
VERITAS.
