- - Sir,—l have readwith interest and pleasure—not tin- ". mingled with hope—the letters on the above subject which have appeared in your journal. We are now getting into the month of May ; there are indications of warm and settled weather, and if anything is going to ihe.done it is a case of now or never. It would hardly he contended, by any citizen, however warrnly-, attached to his native town,that Runcorn possesses many architectural,or artistic attractions, yet it is situate with- in easy reach of some of the most beautiful scenery in England. I think if some of our" City Fathers " would take this matter up, they could easily arrange withthe Railway Company to run us a train or two, say to Fred- sham in the afternoon and back in the evening, so that we might "wander in the merry greenwood, all on a summer's day :"--z-Yours truly. SOLOMON MUGCLICIFLIN.

THE AUTHORSHIP OF THE GOSPELS. Sir,—ln his letter of April 11th, Mr. Dignum says that I have now come face to face with the question atissue ; that after excursions into regions of irrelevant matter, such as inapplicable and imperfect quotations from Mosheim, legends of councils and jumping books, ques- tions as to Renan's-and Huxley's unbelief, and lastly,but most foreign of all--LKingsley's " Hypatia "—it is re- freshing, at length-to meet me in something like a corner. Now to all this I most decidedly demur. I have not ic any case wandered 'from the question at issue, nor have I given either inapplicable or imperfect quotations from. Mosheirn. The quotations have been altogether too ap- plicable, too pertinent to suit Mr. Dignum, and any want , of verbal agreement between his copy of Mosheim and and mine is due, as ',I have already pointed out, to the fact of our respective copies being by different translators. I might with equaljustice charge him with giving im- perfect quotations. Touching Benoit's 'unbelief, it was surely not irrelevant for me to ask why he should be "a most consummate sceptic." Mr. Dignum quoted him with evident ;43- proval, and said he was,a man who had spent almost his life in the examination and sifting of ancient docu- ments. He had had,unusual opportunities of ascertain- ing the truth ; he was a man of immense knowledge and research, and, aocording toMr. Dignum, he believed the Gospels to be serious documents, and yet, wonderful to say, he was a " most consummate sceptic." Surely Mr. Dignum need not be:surprised that I should ask -why. And so with Petifessor fluXley. Starting as a believer,he, after many years' study of the question, finishes up. in his old age by being anAr,nostic. In my own case, after being imbued for forty years with orthodox doctrines, I was led into defending these doctrines, and was thus forced to think about them and examine the authority en which they were based. Then it was that I found that ,my orthodox house was built on shifting sands—and it collapsed. And yet I did not go to such authorities as Renan or „Huxley for information. I went to Dr. Moorhouse, the present Bishop of Manches- ter; to Professor Beet, an eminent Wesleyan minister, who was stationed in Warrington a few years ago, and whose book " The Credentigs.of the,Gospels" was first .put into my hands by my friend Mr. Dignum. I also <went to—that is, I studied the works of Dr. Abbott, Dr. 'Martineau, and Professor Carpenter. Needless to say, these so far from hieing sceptics of the Renan type,areall ministers of the Gospel—everyone of then eminent in bismespective church. And what do they tell us? In an article on the Sunday question Dr. Moorhouse tells us that instead of the fourth commandment being given by God to Moses on Mount Sinai it was merely a survival of sun and-moon worship as it existed amongst the ancient Accadians, three thousand years before the days of Abraham. A statement like this seems to me to seriously impair the authority of the Pentateuch and to quite knock the bottom out of any theory of Inspiration and Revelation. Then Mr. Beet says that that the four Gospels :riad the Acts of the Apostles are anonymous; that the names commonly attached to them do but em- body a very ancient tradition. I had not the slightest idea of this before reading Professor Beet. Remember, I was an orthodox Wesleyan Methodist seeking truth, and I sought it amongst the lights of the church, Need I say, that I was amazed? Professor Beet's statement is con- I firmed by Dr. Abbott' who wrote the article on the tGospels in the Eneycloncedia Brittannica. The fact of any man being asked to write for this renowned work at .once stamps him as being amongst the very highest 1 antliorities that can be found on the subject to be written on. Professor Beet's statement is further confirmed by Dr. 'Martineau and Professor Carpenter, and also by Dr, Wescott, Bishop.of Durham. Mr. Dignum tells us that the bishop says that the Councils accepted the scriptures on the strength of the tradition which had been handed down, and Dr. Abbott in the Encyclopcedia Brittannica kW, po got Dr. Wescott in his introduction to the

Gospels, page 255, says "The earniest account of the origin of the Gospels is legendar.i." Now men of the highest eminen'ce in the Christiart churches are stating these things in books which are r ead only by a few of the most cultured members on. their congregations. Whit I have done has been tnei:ely to place them before a larger and more popular aud.ience, and for this offence somegf my very Christian friends have nothesitated to call me, and to speak of me as, an Atheist. The name, though entirely unwarrant/A, has no terrors for me. At the same time lam not clef ply impressed with the Christ- like charity of these my accusers and erstwhite friends. This merely by the way. And now I turn to P apias. With commendable deli- cacy and good taste- —of which I don't complain—my friend stigmatizes my statement regarding this early Father as a garbled. one, and an absurd specimen illogic. The statement I g aye was taken from Professor Carpen- ter's "First thregi gospels." Now, I maintain that the statement was fa perfectly straightforward one, and as to the absurdity of its logic, why. it is, to use a favourite phrase of Mr. Dignum's, the merest 'fancy. Now what is Mr. Digni_un's argument? -Just this—that the mere fact of Pa',Aas knowing John the Elder, Peter, Phillip, John, ate?". James, constituted him an authority—on the authorinip of the gospels. But why does not Papias tell US soraething If what thesepeople say about the gospels? He nientions only one, John the Elder. But who was Jib n the Elder? History sayeth not. Turning again to the Encyclopeedia Brittaurnea, the Rev. Dr. Abbott says --" To the single evidence of Papias, derived from an 'unknown elder, not mud) importance can be attached, and it is very doubtfu(l,whether the most searching in- vestigations will ever determine with certainty the name of the author or authors of any one of the synoptic gospels." I think after this we may as well dismiss Papias. My friend disputes my-statement regarding Polycarp and Irenteus; andis hardly content to abide by the in- junction to let "Tour communications be yea and nay. He comes dangerously near calling his brother something he ought not todo. -However, I don't want to quibble with him; I merely want the' truth. New first as to Polycarp. rknow all that Mr. Dignum tells us about Polycarp's Epistle to the Phillippians, and I know further that, whilst it is admitted by some critics to be genuine, it is also alleged by others to be spurious. I shall not attempt to-decide the point, but will take Mr. Dignum's assumption that it is genuine to be correct. Mr. Dig- num gives us just the quotations from the epistle that I expected he would do. Put what do they prove? They certainly do not prove that Polycarp knew anything whatever about any of the gospels as such. As I pointed out in my previous letters, the sayings of Christ had des- cended orally and passed from mouth to mouth; and the Rev. Dr. Abbott says that the oral tradition is the one that is generally accepted by the best English scholars. ,I also said that some authorities were of opinion that pos- sibly some pre-existing work such as "The memoirs of the Apostles "had formed the basis of our present gos- pels ; and that it was quite true that passages were found in the works of earlier writers (than Papias and Irenreus) which correspond with passages in the gospels, and that this was notably the case with Justin Martyr. It is the case also with Polycarp, that is, assuming that the epistle bearing his name is genuine. I repeat my former statement that we have not a tittle of evidence to show that Polycarp knew anthing whatever about the gospels as such, for touching their names he is as silent as the grave. Mr.!Dignum says it is not true that Irenreus engaged in controversy with persons who did not acknowledge the fourth Gospel. But Dr. Martineau says he did. Here are the doctor's own words—" He actually does engage in controversy with just such persons (the italics are the doctors) with "Some who of late," says Irenteus; ` do not admit the form of tradition which is according to the Gospel of John." And the doctor says that in- stead of establishing the authority of that Gospel by stating weat he knew on the testimony of Polycarp he resorts to the absurd argument that there must be four 'Gospels because there are four winds and four beasts. And yet he uses such testimony to prove that Jesus lived to be over fifty years of age. In conclusion I re-affirm all my former statements touching the Fall and Atonement. I say that they are ,opposed to an ordinary estimate of a human father. I should think them insulting if applied to me ; but how 'much more so when applied to our heavenly Father whose name is love! And yet, as the Rev. Frank Ballard, an .eminent Wesleyan minister, says—" The atonement of (Christ is preached with a coarse,all-knowing carelessness which makes God our Father to be a merciless Shylock, exacting the last throb of agony from an innocent and 'helpless victim." I rejoice that we have men like Mr. Ballard in our Wesleyan ministry who speak out the truth with-no faltering uncertain sound. lam thankful that we have many like him—here and there—and that they are an increasing number. They are the only sure hope of Methodism in these days of extended knowledge and keen mental perceptions. Again, I re-affirm my former statemeat—That Christ never taught these dogmas. If lam wrong why doe; :not Mr. Dignum refute me by quoting some simple words from the lips of Christ which clearly inculcate them ? This would be much more to the purpose than indulging in bitter and ill-natured invectives against Tolstoi who is one of the noblest and sweetest eharacters that have -ever lived.—Yours truly,
JOHN GANDY.

div.head: LICENSING PROSFCUTION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: LICENSING PROSFCUTION AT RUNCORN.

• Sarah Priss, keeper of Rutter's Vaults beerhouse Brun swick-st.,was summoned before Mr. C.Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of having on the ‘2oth April unlawfully sold intoxicating liquor to two drunken persons named John Sharrock and .John Sargent, and further with having unlawfully permittedidrunkenness.—Mr. E. Wynne Humphries 'prosecuted on behalf of the police, and Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, defended.— From Mr. Humph- • ries's opening statement it appeared that although the defendant was a married woman she held the license in her own name. The beerhouse was - situated in a district of th 9 town where there was a considerable amount of drunkenness, and many persons were brought before their worships from that district, and it had become of serious moment 'to ascertain under what circumstances they had got supplied with drink. About half-past six on Monday evening, the 20th April, Inspector Bowyer and P.C. Worth saw some navvies under the influence of drink, coming up Brunswick-st., and they immediately determined to ascertain where the liquor was supplied. They walked into Rutter's Vaults and in the kitchen found the defendant, her husband, and three navvies, two of whom were very drunk. Sharrocks was actually dozing. On the table in front of the navvies was a quart jug containing a slight quantity of beer,and 1 a small glass called a "tot," which was three parts full. It was the custom to hand this " tot " round from person to person. Sharrock said he had paid for that quart,and Priss, the husband of the defendant, said "I have served them with one quart, and me and the Missis was just saying when you came in that it was time they were going." If a publican would admit that it was time his :customers were . going, the.ir. worships would have no difficulty in coming to a decision as to the state of the two ,navvies. The police had no vindictive feeling in the matter, but felt it to be their duty to ascertain how the drunken- ness of the two was caused, and if the Bench considered this a deliberate breach of the law and not a merely technical breach, the police asked for a substantiil penalty to be inilicted.—lnspector Bowyer add P.C. Worth corroborated this statement, and said they had -several times warned Mrs. Priss as to her manlier of conducting the house.—Mr. Swift for the defence drew attention to the law on the subject and explained that the evidence of the defendant and her witnesses would differ in some important particulars. Before Sharrock and Sargent entered the house, a man named Corbett 1 (the sober man spoken of by the police) came in accompanied by a man named King and another. King ordered a quart of beer, and a tot glass, and these were supplied. Afterwards King and the third man departed, leaving Corbett behind. Business being slack,Priss went into the cellar to stillage some beer, and while he was there Sharrock and' Sargent came in. Mrs. Priss was unable to attend-to business, owing to an injured leg, and she called her husband up and told him the men were not fit to be served, and that he had better put them out. At this moment the officers came in. No drink was suppliedtoeither Sharrock or Sargent. Mrs. Priss had occupied tte house for 24 years without any complaint sufficient to :justify the police in bringing her before the court.—Nrs. Priss confirmed this statement, and was cross-examined at length by Mr. Humphries. Pries, the husband, saidthe never heard Sharrock say he had paid for that quart, nor had he (Priss) said he had served them with a (mat. He denied he had used the words attributed to him by the officers.—George Corbett was also called.—The Bench retired to consider their de- cision, and on returning, Mr... Reynolds said they had de- cided to dismiss the charge of permitting drunkenness, and to convict on the charge of selling. They believed the statemeiiit of the police, and thought these people were served, and also that ;that they were drunk. He inquired if there were any previous convictions.—Swt. Large: No.—Mr. Reynolds:: Then we will not endorse the license.—A fine of £1 and costs, Ll. 45., was imposed. The advocate's fee of 10s. 6d. was allowed.—John Sher- rocks was then charged with being drunk on the pre- mises. He denied the charge, but-said Mrs. -Rutter re- fusedto serve him with any drink. Re was fined ss.and costs.

div.head: RETITItIi OF THE QUEEN.
div.p: RETITItIi OF THE QUEEN.

The Queen returned to England on Thursday after- noon, and landed at Portsmouth at twenty minutes past four, from the Victoria and Albert. Her Majesty tra- velled by special train from Portsmouth, accompanied by the Duke and Duchess of Connaught, and arrived at Windsor at 6.20. The saloon carriage was almost filled with choice flowers which her Majesty had brought from Grasse. Pony carriages were in waiting, and conveyed the Royal party to the Castle.
The English steamer Gwendoline, Captain liarrison, haf3 been totially lost at Cabezzos, near Tarifa.

div.head: TRE EkAMINER. SATURDAY. MAY, 2 1891.
div.p: TRE EkAMINER. SATURDAY. MAY, 2 1891.
CARMEN SYLVA.

The Queen of Roumania, who is known in thel world of letters as "Carmen Sylva,' was born in 1843, and is the daugLter of Prince Hermann of Wed, one of that innumerable ctass of petty German princes whose estates are often invisible. Not until she was seventeen did she make acquaintance with the great N%,orld. She .hen paid a visit of several months to 'Berlin, Rushing

Lay, with her usual impetuo- sity, she 'slipped, and would have fallen to the bottom, had not a gentleman,who was ascending at the same moment, caught her in his arms. It was a fall laden with unexpected consequences, for she had ftyllen into the arms of her future husband. Not, however, till October, 1869, did he unex- pectedly appear at the castle on the Rhine, and remind Princess Elizabeth of the ,desire once ex- pressed to reign over Roumania. Thus it came abont that one of Princess Elizabeth's fairy tales assented real shape. Four times over were the couple married—that is, according to the German civil code, according to the Lutheran (her) religion, according to•the Roman Catholic (his), and accord- ing to the,rites of the Greek Church which is the creed of their kingdom. Arrived at her new home, the Princess at once threw herself with native ardourinto all her new duties. She learned to read .and write Roumanian, she made herself acquainted ~with the needs and acquirements of the land, and BOOR saw that she had not been wrong, when, years .ago, she had aspired after this throne as one which would give her a noble work to do. While keep- ling herself aloof from the entanglement of poll- tics, the results of her endeavours were soon felt more beneficially than those of cannon or diplomatist. She founded schools, hospitals, soup kitchens, convalescent homes, and cooking schools; she encouraged popular lectures; she inoulcated respect for sanitary laws, most heedful in an. Eastern land ; she founded art galleries and art schools. In 1870, the Queen became a mother, and though her child was only a little girl, and ' hence of no value to the land as heir, she was none the less precious in her mother's heart. In 1874, an epidemic of scarlet fever raged in Bucharest, and to this scourge the little princess fell a victim. True to her own doctrine, tf.at "In work—in great rich work—must be sought the comfort for all sorrows," the Queen applied herself yet more strenuously to promote the welfare of her people. She now, too, "first began to take up authorship seriously as a pro- fession. She poured out her woe in song. There stands to-day. in the public place of Bucharest, a fine monument representing the Queen in the act of giving a drink of water to a woundecl soldier. This stathe was subscribed for by the wives of the Roumanian army as an enduring testimonial of their ' love and gratitude for her whom the popular voice now christened "the mother of the wounded." The life led by the Royal couple is one of constant hard work. The Queen usually rises early—often as early as four—and works until eight, the only hours in the course of the day when she can be, as she phrases it, "a woman and author ; " the rest of the time she must be Queen. Both sovereigns had often to talk for twelve, or even fifteen,hours at a stretch, and from this cause the Queen once temporarily lost her voice. When she and the King sit down to dinner they are sometimes so tired they cannot speak a word.

ROW LANCE-CORPORAL W. GOATE WON THE VICTORIA CROSS. We take the following from the "Strand Maga- zine" for April, which is up to the high standard it has set both as to the matter and illustration : I might say I was two years in the saddle, al- most continuously fighting. I was with Sir Colin when he retriok Cctwnpore from the Gwalio rebels. We went to the aid of General Wyndham, who had been repulsed. We crossed the bridge of boats under a heavy fire, but forced our way in. As soon as our brave leader got his men in position, he car- ried everything before him. We could still see traces of Nana Sahib's atrocity in June, and every soldier vowed vengeance. The affair that I was in when I gained my Victoria Cross was before Lucknow, the second time. Early in 1858 the rebels had strongly fortified the place, and it became necessary for Sir Colin to take it. Our regiment had some hot work. It was on March 6 that 1 won the Cross, in action at Lucknow, having dismounted in the presence of the enemy and taken up the body of Major Percy Smith, 2nd Dragoon Guards, which I attempted to bring off the field, and after being obliged to relin- quish it, being surrounded by the enemy's cavalry, going a second time, under a heavy fire,. to recover the body, for which I received the Victoria Cross. 1 will try and describe the fight, and what I saw of it. The enemy appeared in great force on the race-course outside Lucknow, and the 9th Lancers, the second Dragoon Guards, and two native cavalry regiments were ordered to charge. The brigade swept on in grand 'style, and clashed into the enemy. We had a fierce hand-to-hand fight; but our troops behaved splendidly, and at last we broke them up. Then we were obliged to retire under heavy fire. As we did so Major Smith, of the Dra- goons, was shot through the body, and fell from his horse. Failing to catch him, 1 sprang to the ground, and throwing the bridle-rein over my arm, raised the Major on twiny shoulder ;in this manner I ran along-side of my horse for some hundreds of yards, antil I saw the 'enemy's cavalry close upon me. Clearly' couldn't get away with my burden, so I determined to do what I could;for myself. Springing into my saddle, I shot the first Sepoy who charged, and with my empty pistol felled an- other. This gave me time to draw my sword, my lance having been left on the field. The Sepoys were now round me cutting and hacking, but I managed to parry every slash and deliver many a fatal thrust. It was parry and thrust, thrust and parry all through, and I cannot tell you how many saddles I must have emptied. The enemy didn't seem to know'how to parry. . Taking advantage of this, I settled accounts with a jolly lot. 'I was determined not to be taken alive. At last some of the Lancers saw me and came to my rescue. 'Thinking the Major might still be alive, I went again to/rescue him, but it was not until the enemy's forces were driven back that we got his body. After this action, General Sir Colin Campbell, General Sir Hope Grant, and some of the cavalry I officers shook hands with me and complimented me. In regard to the sword and lance, I certainly pre- fer the lance; the lance is so keen, it goes through a man before he knows it. I was always very care- ful.never-to let a swordsman get under my lance, and in fighting with cavalry I made full use of the pennon to bailie an enemy's horse. •The weapons of troops on active service are made as'keen as razors, and it was a common thing dur- ing the Mutiny to see a party of soldiers under the Shade of a great tree waiting their turn to get their blades sharpened and the dints removed, ready for Ile next 'fight with the rebels. Our gallant little army was like a ship cleaving its way through the -sea, for wherever we went, the enemy, like the waters, closed in behind.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

ACCIDENT TO A BOY. On Friiday night Herbert Royle, son of r.c. Roy mat with a,rious accident on the Ship Canal Works, at Runceirn, where he was employed. He was standing on the locomotive, in a position to enable him to look on a waggon which they Were approaching. When a few yards away the engine gave a jerk. Royle lost his foot- ing and fell on to the permanent way, and was badly crushed between the buffers of the engine and wagon. He was at once conveyed to the Latchftord Hospital, where he is progressing as favourably as can be ex- pected.

SALFORD AND THE LOAN. The Salford Corporation discussed the question of the _.oan to the Manchester Ship Canal Company at a special meeting on Monday. Salford had suggested that a clause should be inserted in the bill promoted by the Manchester Corporation offering a third of the three millions required by the company to complete the under- taking. Manehester having ,objected, the Salford Corporation decided, with only four dissentients,to with- draw from offering any assistance. Mr. Lees Knowles has given notice that after the second reading of the Manchester Shin Canal Bill in the House of Commons IT will move : " That it be an instruction to the Commit Tee on the Manchester Ship Canal Bill that they havepower to inquire, if they think fit, whether or not any alteration to the number or composition of the directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Board, by the ad- dition of one or more directors chosen by the Corporation of Salford, may be necessary or expedient, and if so, tp make provision for the same accordingly, and that any petition from the Corporation of Salford relating thereto, presented within not later than seven clear days before the sitting of tke committee, be referred to the committee, and that such of the peti- tioners as pray to be heard by themselves, their counsel, agents, or witnesses, be heard on their petition, if the committee think fit, and counsel in favour of the bill be heard against such petitioners." LATCHFORD, &c. In their present condition, there is much in the woiks on thls section of the canal to interest the visitor. he stretch of country between Stockton Heath and Latch- ford, •which was opened up by the gigantic engine of destruction, the German navvy, is not far from being finished. The German navvy, having long since cern- Ated its task; has departed to create havoc elsewhere., leaving the minor machines to perform the work which yet remains to be done. The mOst imposing fea- ture of the operations in progress at the Thelwall entlis the immense viaduct, which is to carry the Warrington and Stockport Railway over the canal. The briekwork alone is a sight worth going many miles to see. A net- 'work of scaffolding rises from the bottom of the 'canal cutting to a stupendous height above the roadway, and on a platform at the top workmen are engaged in fixing the huge iron girders in position. The girders will be about 120 feet above the bed of the canal, and between the bridge and high water a clear air-space of 15 feet will be left for the passage of tall-masted ocean-going , vessels. At Morris Brook, where the clocks anti sluices ' are being made, the cutting is fully 55 feet deep, hewn out Ot the solid sandstone. Each of the lock gates ,will weigh 2EO tons, and will be moved by hydraulic power. Higher up, the section, at Lymm, the work presents no engineering difficulty except as to the soft materialof the , banks. It is all plain sailing; simply the digging of a trench to the necessary depth, the land sinking there- abouts, so that the banks of the canal need to' be raised and with that view loads of spoil are being tipped' along' the-side of the waterway. The manufacture Of tricks at Statham proceeds, as the trade advertisement 'puts it, with" regularity and despatch," half-a-m ili4on bricks 'being the weekly output.

div.head: AN ARCHDEACON ON FREE EDUCATION.
div.p: AN ARCHDEACON ON FREE EDUCATION.

Addressingthe district wardens and sidesmen on the occasion of his visitation to St. Helens Parish Ohurch,on Thursday afternoon, the Ven.Archdeacon Taylor, of Warrington Archdeaconry, alluded at some length to the subject of free education, and said that to him its adoption seemed inevitable. Whatever political party was in power it was quite clear, and had been for some years, that sooner or later they would :have free education. It was op- posed by many 'people, but both political parties seemed deter Mined to have it, and he thought they would have to submit to what was inevitable. In- stead of opposingit,,therefore, they should endea- vour to prepatelor the advancing tide, and make the best use of :it that they could. He urged that they, as Church people, should insist upon the free use of their own schools for their own purposes after the school hours, and that the interests of definite 'religious instruction were safe- guarded. Any difficulty oould be avoided by the kindness and consideration of all concerned, and he should greatly deplore any popular control of the schools by an elected boardif it meant the intro- duction of discord in regard to religious education. He strongly deprecated any aguabbles about religi- ous education, and in concluding he said he would like to see an educational quataication for the exer- cise of franchise, and thereby make the path of ignorance not so pleasant and profitable, and im- prove the illiterate voter off the face of the earth. If only those had the power to vote and exercise the franchise who had passed a certain standard, the country wouldbe much better off.
tCHURCH -SCHOOLS. INIPORTANI ANNOUNCE- MENT.

he Bishop of London, moving in the Upper House of Convocation, on ThuFsday, for a committee to •watch the Government Free Education Bill,said, althoutzh the terms had not been revealed, he had no doubt, from a great many circumstances that had come to his knowledge, that there would be no pro- posal to interfere with the management of church schools, and they would practically remain vested as at present. The announcement was received with appravat by the assembled bishops.

Among the sufferers by the influenza epidemic are the Duke of., Richmond, Lord Belper' and Lord Houghton. The Committee on Railway Rates had to be adjourned:on Thursday, owing to the inability of the Duke of Rich- mond, tba cairman, to attend.

div.head: BOY DROWNED.
div.p: BOY DROWNED.

Mr. Yates, coroner, hela an inquest at Bollington, Altrineham, yesterday aftetnoon, concerning the death of Albert Holt, aged 16, of 48, Ellesmere-st., Howley, Warrington. The deceased was one of the hands employed on the Duchess Countess packet, and on Wednesday, while fastening a rope on hoard that boat, which was proceeding on her daily journey to Manchester, and as the boat WRS passing through Bollington, he fell into the canal. He was taken out of the water quite dead. A verdict that the deceased was accidentally drowned, was re- turned.

div.head: MR. H. SETON-KARR AT SUTTON.
div.p: MR. H. SETON-KARR AT SUTTON.

The annual meeting in connection with the Sutton Primrose League was held in Sutton National Schools, on Monday night, when there was a crowded attendance, and Mr. W. Webster, ruling councillor, presided. Among those present were Mr. H. Seton-Karr, M.P. for St. Helens; Major M`Tear, Councillor Greenough Messrs. J. 0. Swift, C. Culshaw, &c. Mr. C. CulsAw moved the re-elee- tion of Mr. W. Webster as ruling councillor, Mrs. Webster, dame president, Mr. James Smith, treasurer, Miss E. Finney and Mr. James Woods, secretaries; and the executive ,'council as follows :—Mrs. Birair4 Mrs. M'Phail, Major M"Pear, Miss M'Tear, Mr. Stones, Mrs. Stones, Mrs. Booth, Mr. F. Biram, Mr. R. Newton, Coun- cillor Greenough, Mrs. Burke, Mrs. Royle, Major Camp- bell, and Mr. John Lucas. The resolution was carried unanimously.—Mr. T. Woods (honorary secretary) pre- sented the first annual report, which stated that the work of the league had been of a most successful char- acter. The number of members was 226, and .the finances showed a balance of £4 4s. Did. on the year's working. (Applause.) Mr. Seton-Karr, M.P. in moving the adoption of the report, said they must all be glad that their habitation had been so successful and was financially sound. He considered their record was satisfactory proof that tbe principles they upheld were growing every week in St. Helens, and there was nothing more remarkable during the last eight years than the growth of the Primrose League, which had now become a formidable political organisation in the country. (Applause.) The great danger which threatened this country by Mr- 'Gladstone going over to the enemy had been defeated by the elec- tors of this country, and the Unionist Government was now hard at work in passing the Irish Land B 111„ which was intended to ameliorate to a great extent the troubles in Ireland. The Unionist party has not only pacified Ireland and maintained the rights and liberties of the people, and allowed them to carry on their own business in the way they liked best, and to do what they considered fair and best,but had protected them from the; coercion of the National League, and were now bringing in that most important measure, under which one of the great causes—in fact, the great cause—of Irish cliscontent during the past half century would be removed. The principles of the Bill were approved by all parties.; it was elo-erly asked for and eagerly expected by the Irish agricultural tenants, by the Irish farmers, and by the Irish people generally. (Applause.) Councillor Greenough seconded the motion, which was carried, and allote of confidence in the Government was also adopted. A vote of thanks was tendered to Mr. Seton-Karr, and a miscellaneous concert followed..
THE CHARGE AGAINST CAPTAIN VERNEY. COMMITTED FOR TRIAL.

At Bow-st., London, on Thursday, before Sir John Bridge, Captain Verney, M.P., surrendered on the tharge of having conspired with Eugenie Rouillier to procure Nellie Maude Basket for immoral puposes. Mr. Avory vrosecuted for the looasury, and Mr. St. John Wontner defended. Dr. Hearon said Ite had known Miss Basket and leer family. After her return from Paris she made a statement to him, in consequence of which he communi- cated with the polite. Llbert Young, photographer, deposed to having taken a pi:otograph of Captain Verney, in January. 1889 ; and produced the book with his -name. He then wore no beard. Mr. Horace Barrett,,elerk to the London County Coun- cil, identified the handwriting of letters to Mdlle. Rouil- lier, Ir. Russell, and others as Ceptain Verney's. Capt. Verney attended a meeting of the Council on September 30th, the day when Miss Casket said she saw hint in Bridge-et. Joseph Stevens, hall porter at the Travellers' Club, proved receiving letters in the name of Wilson for the past three years, and by defendant's request he forwarded them to vt.rious addresses—the last te-i Paris. Witness had taken letters from a hairdresser's in Bridge-st. for Captain Verney. He believed they were in the name of Wilson, but twas not certain. Me remembered being given as a reference for a house at il.ensington in 1884. In cross-examination he stated that ;he had also forwarded letters to defendant's wife. Madame Louise Adeline, proprietor of an hotel in the Rue La. Fayette, Paris, said at the end of last year a , woman, whom she afterwards identified as Roullier, , called for letters. Witness afterwards received two let- ters addressed to Wilson,which she handed to the French police, Shortly Afterwards defendant called and asked if she could procure one or two "little girls" for him. He was willing to give a hundred francsand more if wit- ness liked. Witness declined to have anything to do with such proposals. She had seen defendant at her hotel with two English ladies 18 or 19 years of age. De- fendant then had side whiskers and a chin tuft. Witness recognised defendant bomediately at the door of the court% Anthony Rees, hairdresser, Bridge-st., deposed to for- warding letters to defendant during the past nine years. Ths defendant was ultimately committed for trial, bail being inDreased,

div.head: STRIKE AT WIGAN.
div.p: STRIKE AT WIGAN.

A general strike in building trade at Wigan was commenced yesterday morning, when 400 men left work owing to the refusal of the employers to accede .to an application for an increase of wages. - - - -

_ . THE LABOUR COMMISSION. The first meeting of the Labour Commission was held yesterday morning, in the new Committee-roona of West- minster Hall, Lord Hartington presiding. The proceed- ings were confined to preliminary arrangements, and the taking of evidence will not commence before Whitsun- tide. It was resolved to admit newspaper reporters to that sitting. TWO CHILDREN DROWNED.

Yesterday. at Bishop Briggs, near Glasgow, two children, one aged two years and the other eight months, were found drowned in a tub of water, in which their mother, the wife of a miner, named Marshall, had been washing some clothes. The mother had been taken ill with a fit, and while she was lying on the floor insensible the children fell into the tub.
THE NEW RAILWAY. COMMITTEE'S DECISION

Yesterday, Mr. Po!Litt, general manager of the Man- h ester , Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railwav,was the prin- cipal witness heard in opposition to the Lancashire. Derbyshire, and East Coast Railway Bill. He strongly opposed the granting of running powers over his Com- pany's line into Sheffield station, and over the Cheshire lines into Manchester. Asked whether evidence was not given on the Ship Canal Bill in favour of shipping South Yorkshire coal from the canal, Mr. Pollitt said some very extraordinary evidence was given. One of the witness's had a facility for manufacturing millions on paper to an extent he had never seen before. The Committee found that the preamble of the bit was proved, except as regarded that portion of it which asked for running powers into Manchester and Sheffield.
DISASTER NEAR LONDON. COLLAPSE OF A. RAILWAY ARCH. MANY PERSONS INJURED.

A bridge at Norwood Junction collapsed yesterday I morning as the Pullman express from Brighton, was passing over it. Fortunately, the front carriages re- mained suspended on the girder. Mr. W. F. Greverson, of Brighton, broke his left ankle, and the guard, Mark Sayers, was severely cut about the head and face. Several other passengers were slightly injured. The engine, guard's, and brake vans, and several third-class carriages were brought to a standstill just as the bridge collapsed. They remained suspended on the rails, as the woodwork of the bridge and much of the permanent way had fallen into the roadway beneath The rails bent under the strain, but happily, did not give way, otherwise there would have been a terrible loss of life. Several carriages in the rear of the train ran off the line, and in these most of the injured passen- gers were found. The following is believed to be a com- plete list :—Mr. F. W. Greyerson,Powis-grove, Brighton, left ankle broken. Mark Sayers, guard, some cuts on head and face. F. Fergusson, Great Tower-St., slight cuts and bruises. J. W. Adamson, First Avenue,Brigh- ton, ditto. Herbert Webb, Philpot-lane, ditto. Wm. Stratford Wicks, Southwark-st., ditto. Bernhard H. Ward, Crighton, ditto. MAY DAY ON THE CONTINENT. 300 ARRESTS IN PARIS.

AParis telegram says :—/lbout 40,000 troops occupy the town. Cavalry patrolled the revolutionary qaart- ers during the night. Cartridges have been distributed to the infantry. Several ringleaders and 300 dangerous characters were arrested in the night. PARIS, FRIDAY.—The morning opened quietly, but a certain stir prevails in the working class quarters. The central districts present their ordinary aspect. Vehicu- lar traffic is being carried on as usual. Workingmen's delegates from the provinces and several Socialist groups are assembling in the Rue St. Martin, with the object of proceeding with their petitions to the Palais Bourbon. A telegram from Decazeville states that all the men are at work in the ironworks and the mines of the district. RIOTING IN ITALY AND FRANCE. A Central News telegram from Rome says a serious riot arose, yesterday afternoon, out of a workmen's meeting near the Church of San Giovanni. Incited by Anarchist agitators the mob stoned the police. The cavalry charged and scattered the people, but some of the troopers were unhorsed and trampled upon. The rioters also stoned the troops from windows but the in- fantry stormed the house, and the police fired a volley. Many persons were wounded but the number is not known. One policeman and one civilian were killed, a deputy being among the injured. There was also a riot at Florence, several persons being wounded. The police encountered an Anarchist mob at Clichy, and four gen- darmes were seriously wounded.

YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four. MANIPUR AND THE GOVF,RNMENT.—in reply to the Marquis of Ripon, Lord Cnoss expressed disbelietin the report that the Indian Government summoned the Maha- rajah of Manipur and other native princes to a durbar in oilier to have them arrested. The Charities Recovery Bill was read a third time, and file House adjourned at 25 minutes to five. HOUSE OF COMMONS. ' • - The Speaker took the chair shortly after three o'clock. PRIVATE BILLS.—The following bills were considered, and ordered for third reading:—The Birmingham and Henle Marden Railway Bill, the Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancashire Railway Bill, and the Rotherham, Blyth, and Sutton Railway Bill. INDIAN FINANCE.—On the motion of MT. HOWARTH an address was agreed to for a copy of the East Indian Fin- ancial statementior 1891-92. THE MANIPUR DISASTER.—Sir JOHN GORST said the at- tention of Government had been drawn to letters from survivors of the Manipur affair. The SECRETARY Of STATE did not believe the Government of India had contem- plated that the Sennapritty should be invited to a durbar and arrested .; and would be very much surprised if such a step were taken. He could not say whether the Agent acted upon his authority. Papers on the subject would shortly be laid on the table. AN EXPLANATION.—Mr. MAHONY made a personal ex- planation. He had been represented in the Irish papers as violently attacking Irish priests, but disclaimed hav- ng done so. limn LAND BILL.—The House went into Committee on the Land Purchase Bill. Mr. PARNELI, expressed the hope that Irish members would select for discussion only important amendments. Mr.HEALY said the hon.gentle- man had no right to expect anything of them. They re- pudiated him from first to last. Mr. PARNELL rejoined that he should express any opinion he chose, undeterred by Mr. Healy's exasperating remarks. Mr. MAN- oNiir moved an amendment the object of which was to provide that, before the taxpayers of the county were forced by that Bill to give a guarantee, they should • be given the opportunity of assenting or dissenting before special levy was laid on them. After some discussion, Mr. BALFOUR replied to the criticisms on the clause and denied it would have the effect supposed. Mr. JOHN MORLEY supported the amendment, favoring popular control over the expenditure provided by the Anse. On a division the amendment was negatived by 187 to 114.
'TERRIBLE TRAGEDY AT BUDAPEST.

BUDAPEST, WEDNESDAY.—A terrible tragedy was en- acted here to-day. A post office ezaplo.ye murdered his wife, his mother-in-law. and his three children, and then committed suicide by throwing himself into the Danube.
INCREASE OF WAGES TO BRICKLAY-

ERS' LABOURERS, CARPENTERS, &c. On Thursday evening a deputation of the Brick- lagers' Labourers met the representatives of the Masters' Association when the matter in dispute was amicably sealed, the advance of wages -N. per hour were granted. Working hours during the win- ter months being reduced as arranged with the brick- layers and several alterations in the working rules agreed upon, a deputation of the carpenters and joiners were afterwards met. They had applied for an advance of id. per hour.—After a lengthy discussion, an advance of a id. per hour was offered and ac- cepted, and several alterations in the working rules were made, which are to come into operation on the Ist day of June next.

Probate has been granted of the will of the late Sir Edgar Boehm, the eminent sculptor, the personalty amounting to £47,276. Particulars have just been received of a shocking gun accident at Tai Isa Cwrn, a remote Denbighshire hamlet, resulting in the death of a servant girl eighteen years of
age. It is statad that General Booth intends to build a great Salvationist temple in London with the legacy of £60,000 or £70,000 left him by the late Mrs. E. Bell, of Glasgow.

div.head: LYMII.
div.p: LYMII.

-- CHERRY-LANE SION CHAPEL.—The anniversary services in connection with the above chapel took place on Sun- day. The services, morning and evening, were conducted by Mr, Wm. Sanderson, of Liverpool. Both were well! attended. In the afternoon a service of song, entitled "Eva," was rendered by the choir, assisted by some friends and instrumentalists. Mr. IV. B. Ferris, Lymm, gave the connective readings. The collection,which was announced at the close of the evening service, amonnted to £l2 Bs., being the largest amount yet received there.

CONCERT AT LYMAI. On Tuesday evening, a concert of vocal and instru- mental music, was given in the Parochial School. Lymin, with the object of clearing off the debt on the school piano. There was only a Moderate attendance. The vocalists were Miss Newcombe, of Warrington (soprano) and the Rev. G. F. Reynolds (baritone) ; and the instru- mentalists, Mr. Frank H. Crossley (violin). Mr. C. R. violoncello), and Mr. Frank W. Reynolds (pianoforte). The programme wasof a varied and interesting charac- ter. Miss Newcombe in three vocal items calculated to tax the powers of even a veteran concert-singer, gave evidence of the possession of a precocious musical talent which it would be well to foster. With the careful and judicious maturing of a natural aptitude there is, indeed, good reason to look forward to a successful musical career on the part of so young and accomplished a singer. The courage shown by Miss Newcombe in repeating, in part, the exacting roulades of Meyerbeer's "Roberto, o tu che adoro " was certainly to be admired. Responding to a recall for " Bid me discourse," Miss New- combe further over-exerted herself in the song " 0 See! Sad Sea !" by attempting not only the voice part but the absurdly over-wrought pianoforte accompaniment which detracts from any little merit which this song possesses. The Rev. G. F. Reynolds, though not exceptionally gifted vocally, sings with an unaffected simplicity of style which goes a long way towards compensating him. The choice of" The Kerry Dace" (Molloy), for , a baritone is, however, hardly to be commendedand, had it not been for a degree of earnestness and conscientiousness which marked Mr. Reynolds's interpretation of it,this song must have failed to awaken the sympathies of the audience. "The Toilers" (Piccolomini), which Mr. Reynolds es- sayed later in the evening, was much more of a success, and was greeted with loud applause. The instrumental items were listened to with marked attention. 01 the violin solos, Raff's " Cavatina " was, perhaps, the most finished performance, and both this piece and Svensden'S ." Romance" gave opportunity of noting that Mr. F. H. Crossley, as a violinist, excels rather in the pathetic and cantabile movements. Wieniawski's " Mazurka " had scarcely breadth enough, the variations of tempo pro- ducing a halting effect not at all inherent in the piece itself. Mr. C. R. Crossley played the two inorceaux for the 'cello by Popper and Goltermann, in a tasteful and pleasing manner, and won well-merited applause. The two trios for pianoforte, violin, and 'cello, were well per- formed, and from their concerted character gave agree- able variety to the programme. Mr. F. W. Reynolds's pianoforte solos were a host in themselves. Alike in the tender sentiment of Schubert's "Moment musicale" and in the more trying exigencies of Chopin's valse and of Lack's "Saltarelle," Mr. Reynolds proved himself an artiste in the true sense of the word; and it is needless to add that his playing gave manifest pleasure to the audience. Itwill be gathered that altogether a very enjoyable even- ing was spent.

COUNTY OF CHESTER. WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACTS, 1878 AND 1889. BYE-LAWS REGULATING THE SALE OF COAL. NOTICE is Hereby Given, that the following BYE- LAWS REGULATING THE SALE OF COAL within the District under the jurisdiction of the County Council of the County of Chester are new in operation, viz. :- 1. Every person hawking, selling, or exposing Coal for sale by retail, shall cause his name and place of business to be registered at the Head Office of the Weights and Measures Department of the County Council at Chester Castle, and on each and every occasion on which he shall change his registered place of business he shall, within fourteen days thereafter, cause to be communicated to the said office particulars of such change. 2. Every person who shall sell or offer for sale from any vehicle, horse, or other beast of burden, Coal in quantities not exceeding two hundred-weight, shall carry such Coal in sacks, bags, or other receptacles con- taining either two-hundred weight, one hundred-weight, half-hundred weight, or quarter ot a hundred-weight; and the top of every such sack, bag, or other receptacle, shall have permanently fastened to it a metal label in- dicating the correct weight of Coal therein; and no per- son shall sell or offer for sale in sacks, bags, or other receptacles, Coal which is of less weight than that speci- fied on the label attached to such sack, bag, or other receptacle. 3. Every person who shall sell or offer for sale from any vehicle horse, or other beast of burden, Coal in quantities not exceeding two hundred weight, shall carry therewith a correct weighing instrument of a form ap- proved by the Local Authority, and duly stamped by an inspector for this County, together with correct weights, for the purpose of weighing any or either of the quanti- ties of Coal mentioned in Bye-law No. 2, and such per- son shall re-weigh the Coal upon being requested to do so by the purchaser, or by any one on behalf of the pur- chaser, or by an Inspector of Weights and Measures. 4. Every person who shall sell or offer for sale from any vehicle, Coal in quantities not exceeding two hun- dred-weight shall have clearly and legibly painted upon a ccrnspicuous part of the right hand side of such vehicle, in letters not less than one inch in height and of pro- portionate breadth, the name and place of business of the person selling such Coal, and shall keep the same legible and undefaced. 5. Every person who shall sell, or offer for sale, at any wharf, yard,or other place, Coal in any quantity not exceeding two-hundred-weight, and not contained in sacks, bags, or other receptacles, as required by Bye-law No. 2, shall sell such coal in quantities of either two hundred-weight, one hundred-weight, half a hundred- weight, or quarter of a hundred-weight, and shall weigh such coal by means of a correct weighing instrument duly verified and stamped by an Inspector of Weights and MeLsures for this County, and, if required, shall re- weigh Coe same in the presence of the purchaser, or of any one on behalf of the purchaser, or of an Inspector of Weights and Measures. 6. Every person selling Coal in bulk in quantities exceeding two hundred weight, shall (unless the vehicle is provided by the purchaser) cause the tare weight to be marked, and kept marked,in legible figures sr letters, of not less than one inch in height and of proportionate breadth, QA a conspicuous part of the left hand side of the body of the vehicle delivering such coal., 7. Every person in charge of a vehicle in which coal is carried in bulk shall, if so required by or on behalf of the purchaser, or by an Inspector of Weights and Measures, , conucy such vAicle or coal to be weighed or re-weighed lay a duly verified and stamped weighing instrument, provided that no person shall be required to convey such vekicle or coal for a greater distance than half-a- mile, and that such person may weigh or re-weigh the vehicle or coal at the nearest stamped weighing instru- ment which may be available for such purpaso within the prescribed distance of half-a-mile. 8. The penalty for every breach, contravention, or nonobservance of any one or any part of any one of the foregoing ByedLaws shall be any sum not exceeding five pounds. REGINALD POTTS, • Clerk to the County Council. Chester, Ist May, 11391.

-LIOR SALE BY PRIVATE TREATY,. BOLD HALL ESTATE, Freehold, containing about 1.600 acres, with a yearly rent roll of about £3,500; farm rents reduced. The mansion is handsome, having been designed by the eminent Italian architect, Leoni, and very commodious, with exten.- sive stables, coach-houses, gardens, and glass-houses. It is surrounded by lawns and pleasure grounds, woods and plan- tations, and stands in a park of about 250 acres, with three entrance lodges. The estate is compact and the shooting ex- cellent, and good hunting within easy reach. The land is very fertile, and the farms are all well let. There are two public-houses. Several mines of coal exist under the pro- perty. and some of these are being worked within about 40 yards of the boundary. The mines and minerals, and also the timber, will be included in the sale. St. Helens Junc- tion Station, on the North-Western Railway, is 1i mile from the hall, and there are frequent trains to and from Liverpool, taking only 18 minutes, and also from Manchester, occupying half-an-hour for tc e journey, Warrington is distant only miles from the property. A portion Of the purchase money may, if wished, remain on mortgage.—To view, apply to Mr. Robinson, estate agent, Bold Hall, near St. Helens, Lanca- shire ; and for further particulars and terms to him, or to Messrs. NOTES ON GAVES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL.—RUGBY. It seems very likely that Mt. Roland Hill will be able to take out a strong Rugby team to South Africa in June, and the party will probably include several Scot- tish Internationals, such as M'Ewan, P. R. Clause, Goodhue, W. E. Maclagan, and J. D. Boswell. W. G. Mitchell is most likely to go to the Cape, and I dare say we shall hear of R. L. Aston and E. G. North being in- cluded. It is hoped, for the credit of the old country, that the party will be a large and strong one, with plenty of reserves, and composed of men who can put up with a bit of rough work. At the annual general meeting of the Welsh Asso- ciation, held at Wrexham, on Wednesday eight, a recommendation of the Football Association to the International Board that iimpires be abolished and linesmen be substituted was approved of, as was also the 'recommendation that .in case of a player inten- tionally tripping or holding an opposing player or deliberately handling the ball within twelve yards from his own goal - line a penalty kick should be allowed, all players, with the exception of the oppes- ing goal-keeper, standing behind. The "Athletic News" says it is so profoundly itn pressed with the unfairness of the railway companies not allowing clubs to travel at a single fare that it has de- termined to compile a list of mileage covered by the lead- ing Rugby and Association teams and lay it before the combined companies at their next meeting. As a proof of the difference the single fare would make to some clubs as compared with the double fare—it is mentioned that Grimsby Town Club have played 18 matches, and travelled 3,654 miles, an average of 203 miles per match. This, however, is only direct mileage, but if allowance is made for the roundabout way we have frequently had to come home it will certainly be upwards of 4,000.. For instance from Middlesbrough, instead of coming home direct, the only means of getting back the same night night was to go to Leeds and return by an excursion. From Crewe, we left Crewe at 4.30, arrived at Man- chester at 5.35, left Manchester at 8.35, arrived at Wake- field at 10, left Wakefield at 12, and arrived at home at 2.45 a.m., thus spending 71 hours on the railway, after deducting the stoppages at Manchester and Wakefield. ASSOCIATION. A largely attended public meeting was held at Crewe on Tuesday night to consider the position of the Alex- andra Football Club. Mr. Hall. secretary to the football Alliance, reported that Mr. Webb, locomotive superin- tendent of the London and North-Western Railway, had absolutely refused to employ professional footballers in Crewe works. Mr. Webb was asked to receive a depu- tation on the subject, but he had declined, and said any footballers receiving money in future would be discharged from their service. Complaint was made that the club had been governed by one man, and a committee was formed to select an amateur team. Thomas Meadowcroft, aged 21, overlooker, residing at 86, Shaw-road, Newhey, died on Sunday from injuries received in a football match at Gravel Hole, near Roch- dale, on Saturday. The deceased was playing on behalf of St. James's Club, Thornham, against St. Mary's Club. Balderstone, and when running with the ball two of the St. Mary's players tackled him, and Meadowcroft fell, with one of them on the top of him. He exclaimed, "Oh, my neck ; I think my back is broken." Dr. Young, of Royton, was soon in attendance, and the unfortunate player was removel home, where he died on Sunday morning. The doctors are of opinion that he died from injuries to the spine. CYCLING Harris, the young Leicester rider, who defeated Jones and Sansom in the seeond heat of the Surrey Mile Cup, is but 17 years of age. To out-sprint these two noted flyers is a feat of which anyone may be proud.
